vision: Launchway is one place to host your code, build it, test it, scan it and deliver it, on servers you control or as a hosted service.

It aims to be complete without being complicated: every task is a guided wizard, every capability is also in the API, the command line, the agent endpoint and Terraform, and the only things it needs are a database and Git.
AI helps where you ask for it and stays off where you do not, and every Sortie, change and approval is a durable record you can audit.

available.title: Pipelines as code
available.value: Typed YAML with steps, dependencies, run inputs, outputs passed between steps and loops, kept in Git next to the code they build.

available.title: Flow control
available.value: Conditions on steps, retries with back-off, lanes that make runs take turns, run timeouts, and re-running from any step with what each step was given.

available.title: Watching a run live, with time estimates
available.value: Output reaches the page within about a second, image builds print each step as the builder reports it, and each step and run shows how long it usually takes from earlier runs of the same pipeline, with the time left along the longest path.

available.title: Build caches
available.value: Dependencies kept between runs in the database, with entries a pull request can write but the default branch never reads.

available.title: Triggers
available.value: Push, pull request (with target-branch filters, and newer pushes cancelling older Sorties), manual, schedule and webhook.

available.title: Built-in starters and pipelines with no file
available.value: The Hangar: Flight plans and Maneuvers that ship with Launchway. A file can be two lines (uses: launchway/python-service), or none at all and the repository's own files choose one. A service Flight plan checks, tests, audits, scans, builds the image, and delivers to each of the project's Airfields in order, with a decision where an Airfield is protected, a health proof and an automatic return to base. Any stage can be switched off, extended or taken over from the file. A gallery shows each with its inputs and what it runs.

available.title: Shared libraries
available.value: Templates and scripts in their own repository, pinned by tag, branch or commit, with typed parameters.

available.title: Step resources
available.value: Each step is sized, with defaults per kind of step and a ceiling no step can pass, so one step cannot starve a cluster.

available.title: Configuration in the database
available.value: Projects, Flight lines, Airfields, policies, models and more are objects in the database with history, audit and safe concurrent edits, never a file to hand-edit.

available.title: Four levels
available.value: Base, Wing, Squadron and Project (or the plain Installation, Organization, Team and Project), with words you choose and levels nobody uses kept out of sight.

available.title: Guided setup wizards
available.value: First-run setup, connecting a repository, adding a Station, an Airfield, a policy or a verification step: plain questions, explained options, answers checked as you go.

available.title: A guided interface
available.value: A Home page that says what to do next with a setup checklist, navigation whose sections and tabs appear only when there is something to show, and a Sortie page that says why each wait is happening.

available.title: One capability, every interface
available.value: What the web UI does, the HTTP API, the command line and the agent endpoint do too, with a table in the build that fails when one falls behind.

available.title: High availability
available.value: Several servers on one PostgreSQL database with no leader; a Sortie survives a server or a Station dying. SQLite for a single server.

available.title: Quality gates
available.value: Lint, size, architecture, test and originality checks fail the build, so the code stays easy to change.

available.title: GitOps with Argo CD
available.value: Deploy by Git commit, watch sync and health, control Argo Rollouts (promote, abort, retry), roll back, lock Airfields.

available.title: Applications view
available.value: The Argo CD applications a deploy Station has seen, shown with their status next to your environments.

available.title: Verification after a deploy
available.value: Checks on Prometheus, Loki, ClickHouse and OpenSearch with automatic abort or Return to base; an optional model explains the verdict and never turns a failure into a pass.

available.title: Container images
available.value: Rootless builds, scans, signatures, provenance and SBOMs, pushed to any OCI registry.

available.title: Approvals and protected environments
available.value: Approval steps; the person who started a Sortie cannot approve its production deploy.

available.title: Policy gates
available.value: Rules pipelines cannot opt out of, at run start, before deploys and image pushes; report or enforce; audited, expiring waivers.

available.title: Sign-in and access
available.value: OpenID Connect sign-in with groups, roles per project and Airfield, scoped API tokens and an audit trail.

available.title: Secrets that stay with runners
available.value: Pipelines hold references; Stations read values from Vault, OpenBao, files or the Airfield, and mask them.

available.title: Security findings and SBOMs
available.value: Secret, code, dependency, license and image findings (SARIF), new and fixed across runs, and a component search.

available.title: Secure step execution
available.value: Non-root step pods under strict pod security, a step pod removed when its Sortie ends and leaked ones reaped, container and host executors, and Stations that only connect outward.

available.title: Runner identity and pools
available.value: Join tokens, a key per Station, pools scoped to projects, and allow-lists on the Station itself.

available.title: Test, coverage and HTML reports
available.value: Thirteen test formats, coverage with thresholds, flaky-test detection, history, and the tools' own HTML reports in a sandbox.

available.title: Built-in artifact storage
available.value: Cargo and hosted reports live in the database by default, so several servers need nothing else; S3 or a shared folder are optional.

available.title: AI models in steps
available.value: Optional hosted or local models for steps and failure explanations, with per-model token limits; keys never enter a step's container.

available.title: An endpoint for agents
available.value: Agents validate pipelines, start and watch runs and diagnose failures with exactly the rights of the token they hold.

available.title: Open source
available.value: Free software under the AGPL-3.0, with a commercial license for those who cannot use it, and this documentation site with its roadmap.

available.title: A public documentation site and roadmap
available.value: Enterprise-level documentation with diagrams, security guidance, a graphical roadmap with drill-down pages, and a local demo.

available.title: Launchway’s own words
available.value: Two built-in sets of words (aviation-flavored and plain business names), a rename for any word, and the same words in the interface, documentation and messages.

available.title: Learn, inside the product
available.value: The documentation of the release you are running, with pictures and an offline search, opened from the interface with no separate website.

available.title: Variables at levels
available.value: The same variable declared at a nearer level overrides the one above, with locks from above and a hierarchy view that shows where each value comes from.

available.title: Feature toggles (first slice)
available.value: Toggles per Airfield with rules and sticky percentages, reasons and approvals on by default, history with revert, SDK keys, Go and TypeScript libraries, and a toggles file; Returns to base list the toggle changes since the version they restore.

available.title: Shared pipeline templates and Flight plans
available.value: A template or a Flight plan set once for a Wing or Squadron, used by every project beneath it, with deploy, verify and approval steps included.

available.title: Rides through outages
available.value: Database errors are retried, Station writes are safe to repeat, a Station keeps its logs and results while the server is away, and a doctor command checks the database.

available.title: Accessible by design
available.value: Automated scans, contrast tests and keyboard journeys run on every change, with a published conformance statement and a quality bar for the API, the agent endpoint and the command line.

available.title: A failed step says why
available.value: Every failed step states its reason and cause with the evidence, can be re-run from that step, and the actions offered are only those that can work.

available.title: A push starts a run
available.value: A push to a hosted repository starts the matching pipeline, with markers to skip a Sortie, and a minimum Git version checked at install.

available.title: Security scans as gates
available.value: Vulnerability, secret, dependency, image, chart and manifest scanning, fuzzing, an SBOM and security headers run on every change, backed by a security policy and a threat model.

available.title: Pull requests and code review
available.value: Open, review, comment on lines, suggest changes and merge inside Launchway, with merge rules that block until required checks pass.

available.title: Pipelines drawn the way they run
available.value: Steps that run together appear side by side on the Sortie page, drawn from their dependencies.

available.title: Rollback after a successful deployment
available.value: Return to the last stable state even after a rollout has succeeded, with the consequence shown first and a Logbook entry.

available.title: Releases and release management
available.value: A release is versioned, fixed once published, promoted from Airfield to Airfield with the same commit and image digest, checked by a checklist with windows, freezes and Clearance, and reported on with the four delivery measures. Formations promote several projects' releases together in an order you write; a dependency graph will propose the order later. Not yet: the pipeline language has no release trigger or step of its own (pipelines run the launchway command), releases are not signed, and backports are a pull request you open.

available.title: Queues, limits and path filters
available.value: Steps wait for room instead of failing, runs are limited and ordered fairly, documentation-only pushes skip the heavy steps, and untrusted pull requests run restricted.

available.title: The Debrief: test reports, flaky tests and exports
available.value: A report of each run's tests with what changed against the default branch, failures with expected against actual, flaky-test detection from history, quarantine by pull request, coverage of a change, timings and a balanced split for shards, and exports as one HTML file, a PDF, JSON and merged JUnit.

milestones.name: Host your code and run your pipelines in one place
milestones.promise: A team can keep its repositories in Launchway, review and merge there, and run every pipeline it has, with everything a hosted CI service offers and nothing else to install.
milestones.audience: Teams that want one product for their code and their builds, and teams that keep their code on another host but want Launchway to run the pipelines and report back.
milestones.what: Milestone 1 makes Launchway a complete home for day-to-day engineering. Code can live in Launchway or stay where it is; either way people review changes, see every check on the change, and run every pipeline they had on a hosted CI service. The interface follows a change from idea to running software so a beginner can find their way.
scenarios: You push a branch and open a change. The page shows the pipeline running, the tests and findings as they arrive, and a plain sentence saying what stops it from merging.
A teammate suggests a one-line fix in review and you apply it with one click; the checks run again by themselves.
You keep your code on another host. Launchway runs the pipeline and writes the result back to the pull request, and a failing Sortie blocks the merge there too.
You re-run a failed run from the third step, and the first two steps use what they produced last time.
A new colleague opens Home and is told, in order, what to set up next.

groups.name: Host your code
groups.blurb: Launchway stores your repositories and serves them, so one product and a database are enough.

items.title: Built-in Git hosting
items.value: Launchway stores your repositories and serves them over HTTPS and SSH, with storage designed so that no acknowledged push is ever lost.
items.detail: A push, over HTTPS or SSH, is acknowledged only once it is durable, and any server in a group can serve any repository because servers keep nothing that matters on their own disks. This is the Base every other hosting item stands on. Today repositories are served over HTTPS and SSH, and a push starts a Sortie.
items.needs: A database; the shared blob store that already exists.

items.title: Safe storage and failover for repositories
items.value: If a server or the database fails over, every acknowledged push is still there.
items.detail: Refs and their history live in the database with an atomic update, content lives in the blob store, and servers hold only disposable caches. A test kills servers mid-push and the pass mark is that nothing acknowledged is lost.

items.title: Git over SSH
items.value: Clone, fetch and push over SSH with your own keys, beside HTTPS.
items.detail: User keys and per-repository read-only deploy keys are listed and revocable in one place, the server proves itself with a protected host key that stays the same across servers, and SSH uses the same permissions, limits and audit as HTTPS. Run-scoped read-only credentials mean a pipeline holds a credential only while it runs. Today there are user keys, deploy keys, and a key page in the interface.

items.title: Create, rename, archive and set visibility
items.value: The everyday repository lifecycle: create, rename with redirects, transfer, archive as read-only, and private, internal or public visibility.
items.detail: The same wizard connects an existing repository from another host or creates a hosted one, so people do not need to learn two flows. Old addresses keep working after a rename.

items.title: Browse and search your code
items.value: The files of a repository at any branch, tag or commit, with the last commit of each, a README, history, blame, comparing two branches, and permanent links with line ranges.
items.detail: A go-to-file finder (press t), a branch and tag switcher, syntax colors, a file's history that follows renames, raw downloads that can never run in the page, and branches and tags pages. Not yet: archives, and the newest commit drawn on its journey above the file tree.

items.title: Search inside a repository
items.value: Find text, a regular expression or a file name in the branch, tag or commit you are looking at, narrowed by folder and extension.
items.detail: Search reads a disposable copy of the repository with bounded time and size and says when its results are partial, so there is no index to keep in step. Not yet: results for pipeline files, templates and steps as such, and search across repositories.

items.title: Show every kind of file properly
items.value: Markdown, diagrams, math, tables of data, images with before and after, documents and notebooks render in the browser.
items.detail: Pipeline files also render as a drawing beside the text. Rendering is sandboxed so a file can never run anything.

items.title: Edit in the browser, as a commit
items.value: Edit, add or delete one file from the web page; every save is a real commit, on the branch or on a new branch with a pull request.
items.detail: It uses the same one-file commit path as the HTTP API, the CLI and the tools, with the branch rules of a push. Not yet: upload, cherry-pick, revert and patch download.

items.title: Verified commits and tags
items.value: Verify signatures on commits and tags, manage signing keys, and let a rule require signed commits.
items.detail: A verified state is a fact a branch rule or a deployment policy can ask for, so an unsigned change cannot reach production if you say so.

items.title: Repository maintenance and health
items.value: Scheduled housekeeping, an integrity check, a size report and a health note on the home page.
items.detail: Problems appear in the same attention list as everything else instead of being found when a push is slow. Maintenance runs as separate programs, not inside the server.

items.title: Repository trash
items.value: A deleted repository goes to a trash and can come back within a set time.
items.detail: Delete is reversible for a period you choose, and both the delete and the restore are in the Logbook.

items.title: Mirrors in and out
items.value: Pull a repository from another host on a schedule, or push every change to another host as a safety copy.
items.detail: Status, last error and lag show on the home page and raise an alert, so a stale mirror is noticed. A pull mirror lets teams move over at their own pace. Today both directions work, and a stale mirror is flagged.

items.title: Repository settings screens
items.value: Collaborators, access, tokens, webhooks, merge options and feature switches, each as a plain screen.
items.detail: Features that are switched off are hidden, so a small project stays small. Each screen explains what it does in a sentence.

items.title: Branch and tag manager
items.value: List, rename, delete and restore branches, set the default, and delete merged branches automatically.
items.detail: It also shows the last pipeline result on every branch, so stale or broken branches are easy to spot.

items.title: Large files
items.value: Store large binary files outside the normal history, with locks and quotas.
items.detail: Quotas and usage are shown next to the repository. The Station image includes the tooling, so builds fetch large files without extra setup.

items.title: Forks and templates
items.value: Fork a repository to propose changes from your own copy, and start new repositories from templates.
items.detail: A template can carry a pipeline and an Airfield setup, so a new repository arrives with a working path to production. Fork runs follow the rule that untrusted code never sees secrets.
items.needs: Pull requests on the built-in host.

items.title: Repository quotas and size limits
items.value: Limits on repository size, large-file storage and per-organization usage, shared with Cargo and log quotas.
items.detail: One quota model for everything that takes space, with warnings before a limit is reached.

items.title: Activity, language and topic information
items.value: Contributor activity, commit graphs, languages, topics and a repository picture.
items.detail: Delivery information such as deployment frequency and lead time sits on the same page, because Launchway already knows it.

items.title: Webhooks to other tools
items.value: Send repository events to chat tools and any web address, with a delivery log, retries and test deliveries.
items.detail: One notification channel set is shared with pipelines and approvals. Payloads are signed, and compatible shapes are offered so existing tools keep working. Today every delivery is logged with its result.

items.title: Notifications and email
items.value: An inbox, watching and muting, and email for mentions, reviews and failures, including replying by email.
items.detail: Sending mail is optional and off until configured. Email is planned: there is no mail sender in Launchway yet. The same preferences will cover review, work item and pipeline events.

groups.name: Review and merge changes
groups.blurb: Pull requests that show the Sortie, the tests and the policy verdict on one page.

items.title: Pull requests on the built-in host
items.value: Open, review, discuss and merge changes inside Launchway, with branch rules that block a merge until required checks pass.
items.detail: Works in the web interface, the HTTP API, MCP and the launchway pr command. The page shows the latest Sortie's launch line, the required checks and the plain reason a change cannot merge yet. A push prints the address to open one, and git push -o pr.create opens it. Not built yet: pull requests from forks, and tests, coverage change, findings, policy verdict, preview Airfield and deployment on the same page.

items.title: Review with inline comments and suggestions
items.value: Comment on lines and ranges, suggest a change the author can apply in one click, and resolve threads.
items.detail: Comments stay attached to the right lines when new revisions are pushed. Reviewers choose approve, request changes or comment, and the verdict belongs to a revision. Review requests can be added and taken back, to people and to groups. Built on the review-depth branch, not on main yet: several suggestions applied as one commit, files marked viewed (remembered for you and lapsing when the file changes), keyboard shortcuts, a work-in-progress title that blocks a merge, and the pull requests that wait on you in Needs you and in the notification channels. Not built: a pending review kept as a draft between visits, comments on a whole file, a diff that hides whitespace, and a file tree.
items.needs: Pull requests on the built-in host.

items.title: Branch rules and protected tags
items.value: Required approvals, stale-approval dismissal, blocked merges, linear history, protected branches and tags that cannot move.
items.detail: Built: protected branches, required approvals (and from whom), required checks, up to date, resolved threads, no self-approval, stale-approval dismissal and an audited administrator bypass, set in the repository's Merge rules tab, the API, MCP and the CLI. The page says in plain words why a change cannot land yet. Not built: protected tags, linear history, and rules that ask for signed commits (refused, not ignored).
items.needs: Pull requests on the built-in host.

items.title: Code owners
items.value: Name who must review changes to which paths, using people or groups.
items.detail: Built on the review-depth branch, not on main yet: a .launchway/owners file on the target branch maps path patterns to people and groups, is checked line by line with plain messages, shows who owns each changed file, asks the owners to review automatically (all of them, by turns, or whoever has the fewest open requests), and a branch rule can require an owner of every changed file to approve. Not built: owners that are a Squadron or the group that owns an environment, and the owners file checked when it is pushed.
items.needs: Review with inline comments and suggestions.

items.title: Merge styles and auto-merge
items.value: Merge commit, squash and rebase, chosen per repository, and merge automatically when the rules pass.
items.detail: Auto-merge is driven by events, not polling. A manually merged marker handles changes landed outside Launchway. Fast-forward-only merging is not built.

items.title: Merge queue
items.value: Queue approved changes and test the real merged result with the real pipeline before it lands.
items.detail: Built on the review-depth branch, not on main yet: a branch rule can send merges through a serial queue. The entry at the front has its branch brought up to date with the target, is tested by the branch's own required checks on that head, and merges in order; one that fails, conflicts or changes is taken out with the reason and the person is told. The queue shows on each change. Not built: testing several entries on top of each other and splitting the batch when one fails.

items.title: Resolve conflicts in the browser
items.value: See the conflict, choose a side or edit, and finish the merge on the page.
items.detail: Conflict detection runs as soon as the target moves, so the page tells you early.
items.needs: Pull requests on the built-in host.

items.title: Findings and failures on the diff
items.value: Security findings and test failures appear as notes on the lines they concern.
items.detail: The same results feed the policy verdict, so what you read on the line is what blocks the merge.
items.needs: Pull requests on the built-in host.

items.title: Templates for changes and work
items.value: Templates that pre-fill the description of a pull request or work item, and issue forms.
items.detail: Teams keep their expectations in one place and new contributors get a prompt instead of a blank box.
items.needs: Pull requests on the built-in host.

items.title: Pull-request status everywhere
items.value: Report each Sortie back to the pull request as a status and block a merge that does not pass, on the built-in host and on every connected one.
items.detail: Each run is reported back to the pull request as a status that can block a merge, on built-in and connected hosts. Built-in pull requests already show the latest Sortie and the required checks.

groups.name: Work items and decisions
groups.blurb: Track work, decisions and releases next to the code.

items.title: Issues and work items
items.value: Track work next to the code, with labels, milestones, assignees and links between items, and link every change to the reason for it.
items.detail: An item also traces to commits, runs and deployments, so the question which Airfield a request reached has a one-click answer.

items.title: Labels, milestones and templates for work
items.value: Colored and exclusive labels, milestones with progress, and templates and forms for new items.
items.detail: Labels and milestones are shared across projects at the levels you choose.

items.title: Dependencies and parent items
items.value: Mark that one item blocks another, and group items under a parent.
items.detail: A blocked item drops out of the list of what is ready next, for people and for agents.

items.title: Boards that show delivery
items.value: A board with custom columns whose cards show where the change is: in review, building, in a test environment, in production.
items.detail: The board is the same data as the list, drawn differently.

items.title: Decision records
items.value: A question, the options, a recommendation, what it blocks, and the answer with who gave it and when.
items.detail: Decisions are reviewed and answered in bulk in the interface. They are first-class records, so months later you can find why something was done.

items.title: Import and sync from other trackers
items.value: Bring issues in from other trackers, or keep them in sync in both directions while you switch.
items.detail: Six trackers are supported equally. A dry run reports counts before anything is written.

items.title: Optional time tracking and due dates
items.value: Estimates, timers and due dates, off until a project turns them on.
items.detail: Time joins the delivery chain, so effort can be read next to lead time.

items.title: Confidential items and links to the code
items.value: Items visible only to chosen people, and branches started from an item that carry its reference.
items.detail: Confidentiality uses the same permission model as everything else, so nothing leaks across a boundary. The branch name needs no typing to stay traceable.

items.title: A wiki per repository
items.value: A wiki that is itself a Git repository, with history, linked live to pipelines and deployments.
items.detail: Pages can show current status. A vault of notes can stay in step with it (see the Obsidian sync).

items.title: Static pages
items.value: Publish a static site from a branch of a repository, built by a pipeline.
items.detail: The site is served by Launchway with its own address and the same access rules as the repository.

items.title: Releases with notes and evidence
items.value: Releases with tags, notes, attachments and drafts, with notes grouped by work item and marked with where each change reached.
items.detail: A release is a signed record of what was actually deployed, with its images, provenance and approvals attached automatically.

groups.name: People and access on the host
groups.blurb: Accounts, organizations, tokens and administration for the built-in host.

items.title: Wings, Squadrons and collaborators
items.value: Teams with their own permissions on repositories, and invitations for people from outside.
items.detail: One permission model covers code, work items, pipelines and Airfields, so there is no second set of users to maintain.

items.title: Tokens and scoped access
items.value: Personal and service tokens limited to chosen repositories and actions.
items.detail: Tokens use the same audit trail and limits as sign-in sessions. Service accounts are for tools, not people.

items.title: Launchway as a sign-in provider
items.value: Let other tools sign in with accounts that live in Launchway.
items.detail: Useful for small teams that run a handful of internal tools and want one place for identity.

items.title: Host administration screens
items.value: Users, repositories, queues, background tasks, a banner and a maintenance mode.
items.detail: Everything an administrator checks daily is on one set of pages, and it is also available through the API and the command line.

items.title: Compatible addresses and tools
items.value: Clone addresses, push events and read interfaces shaped like the common ones, so existing remotes, bots and editors keep working.
items.detail: This makes moving over a matter of changing a setting, not rewriting scripts.

items.title: Languages and themes
items.value: A translated interface, light and dark, and custom themes.
items.detail: Accessibility checks are part of the build, so a theme cannot ship with unreadable text.

groups.name: Move your repositories in
groups.blurb: A tested path from another Git host, so switching is a step and not a leap.

items.title: Move your repositories in
items.value: Import repositories, issues, pull requests, labels, milestones, releases and wikis from another Git host, and keep a mirror back while you switch.
items.detail: Counts are reported one for one and a dry run shows what would happen first. Moving can be done a team at a time. Today a connection to another host lists its repositories, and each can be imported or mirrored.

items.title: An acceptance suite for hosting
items.value: A written end-to-end suite that hosting must pass before it is called ready, so that switching is a tested step, not a leap.
items.detail: Each requirement a team has of its current host becomes a check, run against Launchway before and after the switch. It is also the proof anyone can read.

items.title: A complete Git forge
items.value: Discussions, snippets, notifications, activity feeds and the rest of a hosted Git service, in order of value, with an interface that is better integrated than a stand-alone one.
items.detail: Everything here is optional and off until chosen. The point is that people who want a single place do not have to give up the usual features.

items.title: Replacing a self-hosted Git server
items.value: A guide and a checklist for retiring a self-hosted Git server in favor of Launchway.
items.detail: Covers moving, redirects, users, hooks, integrations, backups and a Return to base plan, with each step verified by the acceptance suite.

groups.name: Keep your Git host, if you prefer
groups.blurb: Launchway works with the host you already use. Hosting is optional.

items.title: Every Git host, equally
items.value: First-class connections to every major Git host, including GitHub, AWS CodeCommit and self-managed ones, with each one's limits stated plainly in the docs and the wizards.
items.detail: Each host passes the same conformance suite as the built-in one. A host that has not yet passed is labelled so until it does.

items.title: Self-managed variants of hosts
items.value: Hosts you run yourself, with their own addresses and certificates, are first-class.
items.detail: Setup asks for the address and trust, nothing more. Each variant's differences are stated in the wizard.

items.title: Hosts without webhooks
items.value: Hosts that cannot call Launchway are watched through polling or a bridge from their event service.
items.detail: The result is the same: a push starts a Sortie. Launchway posts status as a comment and an approval where the host has no status feature.

items.title: One identity across hosts
items.value: Map the same person on different hosts to one Launchway user.
items.detail: Reviews, approvals and audit entries are then attributed to a person, not to a host account.

items.title: A common provider model
items.value: One internal contract every host, including the built-in one, must satisfy.
items.detail: The built-in host is a provider like the others, so a feature that works on one works on all, or the docs say it does not.

groups.name: Pipelines that match what teams expect from hosted CI
groups.blurb: Everything a hosted CI service offers, in one place.

items.title: Conditions, retries, lanes and re-runs
items.value: Run a step only when it should, retry what is flaky, make runs take turns, and re-run from any step.
items.detail: Re-running from a step keeps what each earlier step was given, so a fix does not mean starting over.

items.title: Warm builds with caches
items.value: Keep dependencies between runs so builds start warm, with rules for who may read and write them.
items.detail: A pull request can write an entry the default branch never reads, which removes the cache-poisoning risk. Cache correctness is being tightened in Build tools and caches.

items.title: Flow control, part two
items.value: Services with readiness checks and logs, a Station and workspace of their own per step, approval quorums, and loops that tolerate chosen members.
items.detail: This completes the control a complex pipeline needs without dropping into scripts.

items.title: Platform matrices
items.value: Run the same steps across versions, systems and architectures from one definition. Available today: for_each combinations with exclude, add, a cap, max_parallel and fail_fast, one log, cache and Debrief for each combination, a grid on the Sortie page, "3 of 4 passed" on the launch line, a pull request check that counts a matrix as one, and re-running one combination.
items.detail: Still to come: values read from an earlier step's output or a file in the repository, and Stations with the right platform chosen automatically.

items.title: Cloud sign-in per step
items.value: Each step proves its identity to a cloud with short-lived tokens, so no long-lived cloud keys are stored.
items.detail: The trust is set up in the cloud once, and the token carries the project, branch and Airfield.

items.title: Re-run only what failed
items.value: Re-run just the failed steps of a Sortie, with earlier results reused. Re-running from a chosen step already works.
items.detail: Combined with caches, a flaky test costs minutes instead of a full run.

items.title: Per-step runner and workspace
items.value: Each step can choose its own image, Station and working area.
items.detail: A step that needs a large machine or special hardware asks for it without moving the whole pipeline.

items.title: Parallel steps drawn as parallel
items.value: Steps that run together are drawn side by side on the Sortie page, so the shape of a pipeline is the shape you see.
items.detail: Steps are drawn from their dependencies, so a Sortie reads like the pipeline you wrote.

items.title: A step's user has an account entry
items.value: The user a step runs as is known to the system inside the step, so tools that look up a user, such as secure shell, work.
items.detail: Applies to steps on Stations and on Kubernetes.

items.title: Runs wait for room instead of failing
items.value: A step with no room in its namespace or on any node waits in line with a plain reason, instead of failing.
items.detail: Built and tested, in final integration; not yet on the main branch. The Sortie page, API and command line say what the step waits for and where it stands in line.

items.title: Run priority and limits
items.value: Set which runs go first and how many may run at once, per installation or project.
items.detail: Built and tested, in final integration; not yet on the main branch. Fair queues keep one project from using every Station.

items.title: Path filters
items.value: Start a pipeline only when the files that changed match, or do not match, paths you name.
items.detail: Built and tested, in final integration; not yet on the main branch. Start a pipeline only for the paths that matter, so a change to the docs does not rebuild the service.

items.title: Steps wait for room instead of failing
items.value: A full step namespace makes a step wait, with the reason, the Sorties that hold the room and its place in line, instead of failing the build.
items.detail: A step that cannot start because the namespace's quota is used up, or no node has space, stays queued with a plain reason and a stable code, is tried again after a growing pause, and fails only after a configurable longest wait (60 minutes by default). A step that asks for more than the whole quota fails at once with the numbers.
items.needs: Nothing beyond what runs pipelines today.

items.title: Limits and a fair order for runs
items.value: Runs over a limit are held with a reason, in a visible order, and the main build is never held.
items.detail: Limits on concurrent Sorties of a project, a pipeline, each kind of run and automation accounts, with defaults that stop a burst of dependency pull requests from starving the main build. Held runs go by priority, an operator can move one to the front, hold it or release it, and a new commit on a pull request cancels the older run of that pull request.
items.needs: Nothing beyond what runs pipelines today.

items.title: Path filters on triggers and steps
items.value: A documentation-only change builds the docs and skips the image and the deploy approvals.
items.detail: paths and paths_ignore on push and pull-request triggers and when: { changed } on a step, with precise glob rules, the previous head or the merge base to compare with, and a Sortie that always starts when the change cannot be told. A skipped step says why and counts as passed for required checks.
items.needs: Nothing beyond what runs pipelines today.

items.title: Restricted runs for untrusted pull requests
items.value: Pull requests from automation accounts and forks run without secrets, deploys or write caches until a maintainer approves.
items.detail: A run from an automation account or a fork takes its pipeline from the default branch, reads no secrets, deploys nothing, saves no cache and pushes nothing to a Depot; a maintainer can choose Run with secrets, which is recorded. The Sortie page says which mode it is in and why.
items.needs: Nothing beyond what runs pipelines today.

groups.name: Easy to start, easy to write
groups.blurb: Write a pipeline from a starter, from detection, or from nothing at all, and have the editor help. Being built now.

items.title: Shared step templates
items.value: Write a step once as a template and use it in many pipelines, with its inputs checked.
items.detail: Being built now. Templates declare what they need and what they offer, so a mistake is caught before a Sortie.

items.title: A built-in starter library for each language
items.value: Ready-made starting pipelines for the common languages, so a new repository starts from good practice, not a blank file.
items.detail: Being built now. Each starter builds, tests and scans; a team can change any part.

items.title: A pipeline with no file, by detection
items.value: Push a repository with no pipeline file and Launchway looks at what it holds and proposes the right pipeline, which you accept as it is or save into the repository to edit.
items.detail: Being built now. The proposal is shown in full before anything runs, and nothing is hidden.

items.title: A gallery of examples
items.value: Browse working example pipelines for common jobs, copy one and see it run.
items.detail: Being built now. Every example is tested, so a copied example works.

items.title: launchway init
items.value: One command in a repository that writes a first pipeline from what it finds there.
items.detail: Being built now. It explains each choice in plain words and never overwrites a file you already have.

items.title: An editor schema for pipeline files
items.value: A published description of the pipeline format that gives completion and inline errors in common editors.
items.detail: Being built now. It is generated from the same definition the server checks, so they cannot disagree.

items.title: Validate pipelines offline
items.value: Check a pipeline, with its templates and shared libraries expanded, on your own machine with no server.
items.detail: Built and tested, in final integration. You can name a library and a directory to check against, and see the fully resolved result.

items.title: More power in templates
items.value: Template defaults derived from other inputs, conditions on every kind of step and optional list entries.
items.detail: Built and tested, in final integration. These close the gaps that forced copy-and-paste.

items.title: Notifications to webhooks and chat services
items.value: Rules that send a signed webhook or a chat message when a Sortie, a gate or a deployment changes, with a delivery log and retries.
items.detail: Built and tested, in final integration. Email is separate and still planned.

items.title: Restricted mode for untrusted pull requests
items.value: A pull request from outside the team runs in a restricted mode: no secrets, no writes to shared caches and no deployment.
items.detail: Built and tested, in final integration. A maintainer can approve a full run after reading the change.

groups.name: A guided interface a complete beginner can use
groups.blurb: Everything by clicking, with every page saying what it is for and what to do next.

items.title: Follow a change on its launch line
items.value: A single line that shows one change traveling from idea to running software, with each station opening its evidence.
items.detail: Choose a station and its review, tests, image, place or decision opens underneath. This is the page that answers where is my change and is it all right. Today the interface is organized around it: Home, Activity, Pipelines, Code, Deployments, Images and Settings.

items.title: A Home that tells you what to do next
items.value: One sentence about what needs you, rows with one recommended action each, and a checklist that disappears as you finish it.
items.detail: When nothing needs anyone it becomes a calm all-clear page with the board of changes in flight.

items.title: Six plainly named sections
items.value: A short, plainly named set of sections, with the ones that have nothing to show kept out of sight, replaces a long flat menu.
items.detail: Anything switched off is not shown, so a new installation is small and grows as you turn things on.

items.title: Overview, then focus, then detail
items.value: Every topic follows one pattern: a picture of what is going on, one thing in focus, then everything about it for engineers.
items.detail: Pages link to each other in context, so you follow a problem instead of searching a menu.

items.title: Nothing lost for a nicer look
items.value: Every detail the current interface shows is kept, and the new one adds to it.
items.detail: Each screen of today has a recorded place in the new layout, and a check confirms nothing has been dropped.

items.title: A do bar for every task
items.value: A search box that finds pages and starts guided actions such as turn a toggle off or why did this fail.
items.detail: It reaches everything without adding to the menu.

items.title: Decision cards that read on a phone
items.value: An approval is a card with what, who, risk, evidence and what happens next, readable in seconds.
items.detail: Reject needs a reason. A decision can be undone until it has acted.

items.title: Pipelines drawn as living lines
items.value: A pipeline appears as stations on tracks, with parallel steps splitting and joining, live while it runs.
items.detail: Parallel steps are already drawn side by side on the Sortie page. The rest, stations on tracks with live motion, is still to come.

items.title: Light, dark and phone widths
items.value: The same interface in light and dark and on a phone, with an accessibility check as a build gate.
items.detail: Charts say where they came from and never rely on color alone.

groups.name: Move your existing pipelines over
groups.blurb: Bring pipelines across in waves, without surprises.

items.title: A converter and a move-over guide
items.value: Bring pipelines written for other CI services across in waves, with a report of anything that needs a person.
items.detail: The converter says what it could not translate, and why. The guide covers running both side by side while you compare results.

items.title: Run old and new side by side
items.value: Compare a Launchway run with the run it replaces and see where results differ.
items.detail: This is how a team gains confidence before switching.
items.needs: A converter and a move-over guide.

groups.name: Foundations that finish alongside
groups.blurb: The groundwork that every other item stands on.

items.title: Terraform provider
items.value: Every kind of setting managed as code, each new kind shipping with its resource, so nothing is reachable only by clicking.
items.detail: A test fails the build when an object exists without its Terraform resource. The provider ships beside the server.

items.title: Database failover and no lost push
items.value: High availability that covers the database and repository storage as well as the servers.
items.detail: Failover is rehearsed in tests with writes in flight. Today the application side rides through an outage; the database side is Milestone 10.

items.title: Launchway builds and deploys itself
items.value: Launchway is built, tested, signed and rolled out by Launchway, in a group of servers, with rollouts and checks.
items.detail: Stations on virtual machines and customer machines update themselves too (see the Station update item). The pipeline and the runbook are written and checked; a first real run, with its Return to base, is still to come.

items.title: Fewer concepts to learn
items.value: No pile of connectors, services and Airfields to define before anything works.
items.detail: Six words cover everyday use: project, pipeline, step, run, Airfield and Station.

items.title: Signed releases and installers
items.value: Reproducible release builds with SBOMs, deb and rpm packages, an install script for Stations and a runner-only Helm chart, with signing and provenance in the release workflow.
items.detail: All of it has been exercised on a machine of its own. The release workflow has not yet run for real, so no release is published; until then, build from source.

items.title: Test like the pipeline
items.value: Run Launchway's own checks locally in the same containers the pipeline uses, so a change that passes locally passes there.
items.detail: The local run gives each step the same user and files as the server run.

groups.name: Install Launchway in minutes
groups.blurb: One command and a few plain questions on a laptop, a server or Kubernetes, then a guided first sign-in in the browser. Nothing else is assumed to be installed.

items.title: A few values and nothing else
items.value: The chart starts a secure working installation from about ten lines or fewer: the address, the database choice and high availability on or off.
items.detail: Being built. Everything else is a secure default or is set in the product after first sign-in.

items.title: Secrets made once and kept
items.value: The chart creates the root key, the database password and the first administrator’s setup once, and keeps them across upgrades.
items.detail: Rehearsed on a throwaway cluster: the install hook Job made the root key once and left the Station token and the database password it found; installing again, and upgrading with unchanged values, kept them.

items.title: Secure by default in the chart
items.value: Default-deny network policies, restricted pods and no public exposure come with the chart, so no folder of hand-written policy files is needed.
items.detail: Sign-in is required, secrets are sealed under a root key, the network policies deny by default and the pods run restricted; checked in a rehearsal on a throwaway cluster, fresh and as an upgrade with unchanged values.

items.title: One-time setup code and built-in accounts
items.value: A new installation requires sign-in from the first moment and offers a built-in first administrator with a second step.
items.detail: Being built: a one-time setup code is printed once, and the rest happens in the browser.

items.title: One command, three targets
items.value: launchway install asks the same few plain questions for a laptop, a single server or Kubernetes, and ends by printing the address and the one-time step.
items.detail: Being built. It is safe to run again and never regenerates keys.

items.title: Asks before it touches a cluster
items.value: On Kubernetes the installer shows the cluster it will change and asks by name, then writes a small values file and runs Helm, or writes files to commit where a GitOps controller manages the cluster.
items.detail: Being built.

items.title: A first-run wizard
items.value: After first sign-in a wizard names your organization, sets sign-in, shows encryption status, backs up the root key, adds a Station and Git hosting, imports repositories and starts a first pipeline.
items.detail: Being built: the remaining steps. A new sign-in provider is tested before sign-in is switched to it.

items.title: A security checklist at the end
items.value: The installer finishes with a plain checklist of what is protected and what to do next, and the doctor repeats it later.
items.detail: Being built.

items.title: Nothing else to install
items.value: The installer carries the chart, the exact image references of its own release and what it needs to talk to a cluster, so no other tool is required.
items.detail: Being built. A release image already carries the chart.

items.title: A small Kubernetes on a server with none
items.value: On a server with no cluster the installer offers to run Launchway by itself or to set up a small bundled Kubernetes.
items.detail: Next in line after the three targets.

items.title: Every cluster feature checked
items.value: On an existing cluster the installer checks storage, a way in, certificates, a name, policy enforcement and rights, and offers a fix or a labeled trial option for each one missing.
items.detail: Never a dead end; anything not yet built is shown as coming.

items.title: An offline bundle
items.value: One file with everything Launchway needs, for networks with no internet.
items.detail: The same walk-through, ending in the browser.

milestones.name: Deeper pipeline power, and a way off self-hosted automation servers
milestones.promise: Pipelines can be as dynamic as real code needs, and a team running an automation server can move its jobs without losing what it relies on.
milestones.audience: Teams whose pipelines need real code, many repositories sharing logic, or a move away from a self-hosted automation server.
milestones.what: Milestone 2 makes pipelines as dynamic as real code needs without giving up checking. Steps become programs you test, pipelines can be generated, conditions are typed, and you can design visually. Teams on automation servers get a tested gap analysis and an importer.
scenarios: You write a deployment step in the language your team already uses, test it on your laptop, and share it as a pinned version.
A step looks at the repository and prints the extra steps it needs; Launchway checks them and shows them on the Sortie.
You drag a step onto a pipeline and see the exact lines it will change in Git before you save.
A message on a Holding pattern starts a pipeline, and a rejected message is visible with the reason.
You import jobs from an automation server and read a report of what needs a person.

deepDives.title: The developer experience and the golden path

groups.name: Write pipelines your way
groups.blurb: Pipelines as real programs, checked before they run.

items.title: Custom steps in your own language
items.value: A step is a program in your repository with typed inputs, outputs and secrets, runnable and testable on its own, so pipeline logic is ordinary tested code.
items.detail: You write the step in a language you already use and unit-test it like any application. A template is the interface and the code is what runs.

items.title: A step contract and starter kits
items.value: A published contract for what a step receives and returns, with starter kits for common languages.
items.detail: Starter kits include the types, a local test harness and an example, so the first step takes minutes.
items.needs: Custom steps in your own language.

items.title: Steps run in a sandbox
items.value: Custom steps run in an isolated container with only the secrets and network they declared.
items.detail: A shared step cannot read what it was not given, which makes sharing steps across teams safe.
items.needs: Custom steps in your own language.

items.title: Share and pin steps and templates
items.value: Publish a custom step, not only a template, from a repository and pin users to a tag, branch or commit. Pinning templates this way already works.
items.detail: Releases are plain Git tags, so versions, history and review use the tools you already have.

items.title: Generated pipelines
items.value: A step can print more steps in any language; Launchway checks them against the same schema and policy and shows them on the Sortie.
items.detail: This gives the freedom of a script with the safety of a checked definition, and it makes dynamic pipelines possible without file-first configuration.
items.needs: Custom steps in your own language.

items.title: Expressions for conditions
items.value: A small typed expression language with no loops and no side effects, checked before the Sortie; today's conditions keep working.
items.detail: Because expressions cannot loop or change anything, a pipeline is always checkable without running it.

items.title: Typed outputs between steps
items.value: A step declares what it passes on, and a reference to an output that does not exist fails before the Sortie, not in the middle of it.
items.detail: Types make the earlier values on a re-run knowable, which keeps restarting from a step honest.

items.title: A browsable catalog of templates and steps
items.value: Shared libraries pinned by tag already work; the catalog lets you find, compare and update them from inside the product.
items.detail: Each entry shows who uses it, what it needs and which version is current, with an update shown as a change you can review.

items.title: Update notices for shared libraries
items.value: See which projects use an old version of a template and open an update as a reviewable change.
items.detail: Teams keep common pipeline logic current without a manual hunt.
items.needs: A browsable catalog of templates and steps.

items.title: A triggers page
items.value: One page showing every trigger and exactly which pipelines it starts.
items.detail: You can answer what starts this pipeline and what does this trigger start without opening files.

items.title: Event sources from queues and buses
items.value: Start pipelines from message queues and event buses, with filters, and replies back.
items.detail: Filters, retries and a dead-letter view show what arrived and what was ignored.

items.title: Steps as a graph of containers
items.value: Lay steps out as a graph of containers with fan-out and join, for work that is not a straight line.
items.detail: Each node shows its own logs and result, and the graph is the same object whether drawn or written.
items.needs: Custom steps in your own language.

items.title: Runners that keep themselves updated
items.value: Stations on VMs and on customers' machines update under your policy, so the fleet never drifts.
items.detail: Hosted pools update automatically, self-hosted pools are notified, and Kubernetes Stations follow the chart.

items.title: Pipeline history and flaky tests
items.value: Duration charts, pass rate and the slowest steps across runs, and flaky tests flagged on the pull request. Flaky detection and test history already work on the Sortie page.
items.detail: Flaky tests are marked on the Sortie and on the pull request, so they are quarantined instead of argued over.

items.title: Step pages
items.value: Each step has a page: where its code lives, its inputs and types, and which pipelines use it.
items.detail: Before changing a step, you see who it would affect.
items.needs: Custom steps in your own language.

groups.name: Builds use every machine sensibly
groups.blurb: A team’s machines share the work by what is free, and nobody’s laptop is taken over.

items.title: Builds placed by free processor and memory
items.value: A build can run on any of a team’s machines and is placed on one with room for it.
items.detail: Today a Station takes work when it has a free slot; placement by what is really free comes next.

items.title: Runners on personal machines hold back when busy
items.value: A Station on a laptop or workstation stops taking work while the machine is busy, and respects the limits its owner sets.
items.detail: This is the first piece of placement to be built, because it makes lending a personal machine safe.

items.title: A build’s parallel steps spread across machines
items.value: The parallel steps of one build can run on different machines, with their shared files moved safely between them.
items.detail: The pipeline stays one pipeline, drawn as it is; only where each step runs changes.
items.needs: Builds placed by free processor and memory.

items.title: Size hints for steps
items.value: A step can say how much processor and memory it needs, and Launchway uses that, and what it has learned from earlier Sorties, to place it.
items.detail: The hints are advice; a wrong hint wastes time but never breaks a build.
items.needs: Builds placed by free processor and memory.

items.title: Windows and macOS runners
items.value: Stations that run on Windows and macOS, so a matrix can cover them and desktop builds have a place to run.
items.detail: This is a gap, listed honestly.

items.title: Fair use between the people lending machines
items.value: Work is shared out so that no one person’s machines carry the whole team, and everyone can see how much each machine did.
items.detail: The report is about machines and fairness, never a ranking of people.
items.needs: Builds placed by free processor and memory.

groups.name: Reports people want to read
groups.blurb: Test results that are a pleasure to read and easy to hand to someone else.

items.title: Polished test reports as HTML and PDF
items.value: Every run can produce a detailed, well-laid-out Debrief as a web page and as a PDF that can be sent to someone without an account.
items.detail: Builds on the thirteen test formats and coverage already available.

groups.name: Design visually
groups.blurb: Draw it, read it as text, and see that both are the same thing.

items.title: A visual pipeline designer
items.value: Drag built-in and custom steps into place; it edits the same pipeline file as the text editor, so the two are views of one thing.
items.detail: The designer shows the lines it will change in Git before you save, and saving is a reviewable change. Nothing is stored outside the file.

items.title: A drawing canvas and diagrams
items.value: Architecture diagrams drawn in Launchway beside generated ones and Mermaid.
items.detail: Diagrams are saved as files in Git and exported safely, so documentation and architecture drawings live beside the code.

items.title: Generated architecture views
items.value: Views of your delivery and runtime drawn from what Launchway knows, always current.
items.detail: Applications, pipelines and Airfields appear as diagrams you can paste into a document.

items.title: Two-way Obsidian sync
items.value: Export and import documents, and keep an Obsidian vault in step with Launchway documents in both directions.
items.detail: A plug-in is provided if the sync needs one. Conflicts are shown, not hidden.

groups.name: Move off a self-hosted automation server
groups.blurb: Everything teams rely on such a server for, without its weaknesses.

items.title: A verified gap analysis
items.value: A tested list of what teams rely on automation servers for (dynamic pipelines, extensions, agents anywhere) with a plan for each gap.
items.detail: Each gap names the Launchway feature that closes it and a test that proves it.

items.title: Import of existing jobs
items.value: Convert job definitions and shared libraries, with a report of what needs a person, and none of the file-first configuration or fragile plug-ins.
items.detail: The import produces ordinary pipelines in Git and tells you what it could not convert.

items.title: Extensions without fragility
items.value: A step catalog and typed custom steps instead of plug-ins that run inside the server.
items.detail: Nothing a team adds can crash or compromise the server, and every extension has a version and an owner.
items.needs: Custom steps in your own language.

items.title: Agents anywhere
items.value: Guidance and checks that show Stations on any machine, in any network, replace the build agents teams rely on. Stations that connect outward, with pools and labels, already work.
items.detail: Equivalent to the build agents teams rely on, with identity and audit on every connection.

groups.name: Share and reuse across projects
groups.blurb: The right amount of sharing at the right level, with the fewest new ideas to learn: a template is an interface, code is what runs, and a nearer level always wins.

items.title: Templates and Flight plans by level
items.value: Set a template or a Flight plan at the Wing or Squadron and every project beneath it uses it.
items.detail: Today a Flight plan can be bound at a level and a project can override what the level allows. A solo developer never has to open any of this.

items.title: Overrides, locks and the hierarchy view
items.value: Declare a variable lower down to override it, let a level above lock it, and see where each value comes from while building a pipeline.
items.detail: Today the hierarchy shows each variable’s source, what it overrides and what is locked, and every Sortie records the values it used.

items.title: Templates that read like code
items.value: A template says what it needs and offers, can be built on another, and a project fills in or overrides only what is open.
items.detail: You will be able to see at a glance what a template fixes and what it leaves open, the way an interface and a class work in code.
items.needs: Shared pipeline templates and Flight plans.

items.title: Language starters
items.value: Starter templates for common languages that set up best practice, naming standards and help for your AI coding assistants. Available today: built-in Flight plans for Go, Python, Node, Java, images, static sites and Helm charts, and a repository with no pipeline file runs the one that fits.
items.detail: Everything in a starter can be overridden; the default simply guides. Delivery runs for plain manifests and Helm values through GitOps write-back; it was exercised offline and against fakes, not yet end to end with a real image build and cluster. Still to come: assistant instruction files, formatter and linter configuration and a test layout written into the repository, findings of the analysis in the Security tab, bandit for library-only repositories, values read from an earlier step's output, and more languages.

items.title: Light environments and services
items.value: Airfields and services as short lists with sensible defaults, not another set of ideas to learn before anything works.
items.detail: You will be able to start with one Airfield and grow, with locks and defaults coming from the level above.

items.title: Shared connections
items.value: A connection to a Depot, a cluster or a cloud set up once at a level and used below it, with its use shown.
items.detail: Secrets stay where they are; only the name of the connection is shared.
items.needs: Overrides, locks and the hierarchy view.

items.title: See what is shared and who uses it
items.value: For any template, library or connection, a list of every project that uses it and what would change if it changed.
items.detail: A change to something shared is previewed before it is applied.
items.needs: Templates and Flight plans by level.

groups.name: Every popular build tool, with a cache that is never stale
groups.blurb: A cache may only make a build faster, never change its result. Build tools become ready-made recipes that work out the cache for you.

items.title: The cache rule
items.value: A build never silently uses an older copy of something it asked for the latest of, and a cache never changes what a build produces.
items.detail: Being built: the rule, the cache key and how it is checked. Where Launchway cannot promise it for a path, the Sortie says so and names the path.

items.title: Fixed things reused, moving things looked up again
items.value: Released versions, pinned images and locked dependencies are reused; snapshots, ranges and latest are re-checked on every build.
items.detail: Being built. A re-check is a cheap lookup, not a download.

items.title: Every restore is a head start, never the answer
items.value: What a cache restores seeds the build and the tool still checks it, so a stale folder cannot decide the result.
items.detail: Being built, with generations and a maximum age.

items.title: Warnings for unsafe cache patterns
items.value: Validation and the pipeline editor flag cache settings that could serve stale or secret data, and propose a fix.
items.detail: Being built.

items.title: Caches by trust scope
items.value: What a pull request writes only that pull request reads; what a trusted branch writes the project reads; forks are isolated; image caches follow the same scopes.
items.detail: Being built.

items.title: What the run restored, and how old
items.value: Every Sortie shows what it restored, how old it was, what it re-checked, and either “this build used no stale inputs” or the exact list it could not verify.
items.detail: Resolved versions are recorded, for example “resolved a snapshot to the build published four minutes ago”.

items.title: Build twice and compare
items.value: Run a build with and without cache and compare the results, or run without cache, or refresh the cache, with one choice.
items.detail: Also the self-test that deleting every cache never changes what a build produces.

items.title: Recipes for the popular tools
items.value: Maven, Gradle, npm, pnpm, yarn, Go, Python (pip, uv and Poetry) and container images are detected, get a ready Flight plan, a correct cache and Debriefs.
items.detail: No hand-written cache keys. First phase of the recipes.

items.title: Shared build caches Launchway hosts
items.value: Where a tool has a build cache that verifies its inputs, such as Gradle, Bazel and container layers, Launchway serves it itself instead of copying folders around.
items.detail: Output folders that depend on file times are not restored across commits unless you opt in.

items.title: More build tools
items.value: Bazel, sbt, .NET, Rust, C and C++, Ruby, PHP, Helm and Terraform follow the first recipes.
items.detail: Later phases.

items.title: Android builds
items.value: Android projects build with Gradle recipes, signing keys kept on your side, and results on the launch line.
items.detail: Follows the Gradle recipe.

items.title: iOS and macOS builds
items.value: Apple projects build on macOS Stations you provide, with signing kept on your side.
items.detail: The honest constraint: Apple builds need Apple hardware.

items.title: Cross-platform mobile frameworks
items.value: Each cross-platform framework says which Station it needs, so a build lands on the right machine.
items.detail: Follows Android and iOS.

groups.name: The developer comes first
groups.blurb: Whatever Launchway can do to help a developer ship the next feature quickly and safely, it does, in the editor, the terminal, the assistant and the pull request.

items.title: An editor extension
items.value: A VS Code extension shows your work, the launch line, run details and logs, and findings as problems in the file, with sign-in from the editor.
items.detail: Built on one editor-neutral core, so other editors can follow.

items.title: A language server and a schema for pipeline files
items.value: Pipeline files get completion and inline checks in any editor that speaks the language-server standard.
items.detail: The schema half is being built now (see the editor schema in Milestone 1); the language server follows. Both are generated from the same parser the server uses, so they cannot disagree.

items.title: Assistant tools shaped by jobs
items.value: AI coding assistants get tools for jobs such as explaining a failure, checking a pull request and opening one, instead of one tool per API call.
items.detail: Each assistant is exactly as powerful as its user and no more.

items.title: Instruction files kept current
items.value: Starter files that tell AI coding assistants your conventions are generated and kept up to date, and every one can be overridden.
items.detail: Language starters carry good practice and naming standards.

items.title: Run it locally, the same way
items.value: launchway run uses the same step images, recipes and cache rules as the server, with a local cache that follows the same freshness rules.
items.detail: The command line already runs a pipeline on one machine; local caches come next.

items.title: Reproduce a failed step
items.value: Copy one command that reruns a failed step with the same image and inputs, or open a time-limited, recorded debug session in a fresh copy of its Airfield.
items.detail: Never with production secrets.

items.title: Flaky tests quarantined, with an owner
items.value: A flaky test still runs and reports but stops blocking, with an owner and an expiry, and a failure says whether it is new or known.
items.detail: Retry only the failed tests, using each tool’s own option.

items.title: A preview environment for every pull request
items.value: An Airfield that expires by itself and has a cost cap, with its link posted on the pull request.
items.detail: A mobile equivalent is an install link per pull request.

items.title: Why is my run waiting
items.value: One answer to why something is not moving: no Station with the capability, a Sortie ahead, a lock, an approval, a quota.
items.detail: Being built with waiting for room; the rest follows.

items.title: First signal fast
items.value: A time budget for the first result on a pull request, with fast checks first and deep checks later.
items.detail: Default: two minutes to the first result.

items.title: A first green build in ten minutes
items.value: Detect the tool, apply the recipe and its Flight plan, and get a green build, with the clock as a test.
items.detail: Includes mobile templates.

items.title: Team metrics, never people rankings
items.value: Lead time, failure rate, time to restore, queue time and flaky rate for teams; an individual sees only their own numbers.
items.detail: No per-person ranking anywhere.

milestones.name: Delivery and GitOps depth
milestones.promise: See and control everything you run, whether it is an application in a cluster, a virtual machine or an image-based host, and deliver to it safely.
milestones.audience: Teams that deploy to Kubernetes, virtual machines, machine images and clouds, and people who answer for what is running and whether it is healthy.
milestones.what: Milestone 3 is about everything after the build. See every application and host in one place, find out why a deployment failed, roll out safely with weights and checks, run infrastructure as code with state kept for you, manage image-based hosts, and watch traffic, protection and reliability in the same views.
scenarios: A deployment fails. Launchway says in one sentence why, shows the evidence, and offers to roll back the setting that caused it.
You send ten percent of mobile traffic to a new version and watch errors on a map before widening it.
You turn off a misbehaving feature with one button on a page that also shows its effect.
A fleet of image-based hosts upgrades in batches with a check between each, and one batch pauses.
A reviewer sees an automatically written change record with its risk and freeze status.
