groups.name: Applications and rollouts
groups.blurb: See and control everything you run, then deliver to it safely.

items.title: Argo CD in depth
items.value: Application hierarchy views (app-of-apps and ApplicationSet trees) with status, sync, health, history and actions, ready health checks, and a hosted or your own Argo CD.
items.detail: Launchway reads each application as the deploy engine sees it, shows drift, and lets you act with the same permissions as everything else. Argo CD is first-class, never required.

items.title: Applications and ApplicationSets from the interface
items.value: Generate applications and sets, and compose app-of-apps, from a guided screen.
items.detail: The generated manifests are shown as a change you review and merge, so GitOps remains the record.

items.title: Health checks set up from the interface
items.value: Write and test custom health checks for resources without editing configuration by hand.
items.detail: A check shows its result against live resources before you save it.

items.title: Hosted or your own Argo CD
items.value: Use an Argo CD that Launchway runs for you, or connect one you already have.
items.detail: Both are equal in the interface. Teams that do not use Argo CD can use built-in deploys instead.

items.title: Rollout control inside a run
items.value: A pipeline watches a rollout, pauses at gates, promotes or aborts, and shows each step of the rollout as a station.
items.detail: Verification tests run between steps, and the Sortie keeps the evidence. Today the commands shown are the ones that really work, and a failed command says so.

items.title: A single pane of glass
items.value: One fleet view of every application and every host: what runs where, its health, drift and evidence.
items.detail: Error rates, version, last change and owner are on one screen, and each tile opens the page that explains it.

items.title: Weighted canaries and traffic control
items.value: Send a share of traffic, by client type, to a new version through the Gateway API or a service mesh, with mesh metrics as ready-made health checks.
items.detail: The overlay on the traffic map shows what share each version takes right now.

items.title: Releases across services
items.value: Ship several services as one ordered, gated release with a promotion view across Airfields.
items.detail: Promotion moves the same digest, never a rebuild, and every step shows who approved it.

items.title: Promotion across environments
items.value: Move a version from one Airfield to the next with checks and approvals in between.
items.detail: The matrix shows what runs where, which places are behind, and a button to move a version.

items.title: Post-deploy watch and incidents
items.value: Keep watching after release, roll back automatically, and tie incidents to the change that caused them.
items.detail: An incident links back to the commit, run and setting change nearest to it. The watch, the stable state and the automatic return are detailed in Milestone 8.

items.title: AI analysis as an optional rollback gate
items.value: Let a verification step use AI analysis of metrics and logs to trigger automatic Return to base, off by default and able to require a person for production.
items.detail: Plain threshold checks remain the default, and AI can decide only where you allow it.

items.title: An HTTP health proof for verifying deployments
items.value: Verify a deployment by having the deploy Station call an address you name over HTTP or TCP and check the answer, with no metrics store needed.
items.detail: Built and tested, in final integration; not yet on the main branch.

items.title: GitOps write-back to a hosted repository
items.value: After a build, Launchway writes the new version into the Airfield repository for the GitOps controller to pick up, by a direct push or by a pull request, using a credential that belongs to that one deployment.
items.detail: Built and tested, in final integration; not yet on the main branch. The image tag and its digest are written together, and a race with another writer is retried safely.

items.title: A health proof built into verification
items.value: A verify step can call the service it just deployed, over its window, with no monitoring series to set up; a failure says how many requests got which answer.
items.detail: HTTP and TCP checks from the deploy Station, limited to the hosts and namespaces its operator lists; credentials are secret references. gRPC health checks are not built in yet.

items.title: GitOps write-back done right
items.value: Several pipelines may write one manifest at once, a tag can sit beside its digest, and a repository Launchway hosts is written with a credential made for that one deployment, directly or by pull request.
items.detail: Not yet: returning to base several deployments at once by pull request.

items.title: Delivery notifications
items.value: An approval that waits, a failed Sortie or deployment, a Return to base and a step that waited too long are told to a signed webhook or a chat channel, with a delivery log and retries.
items.detail: Email, per-person muting and a Return to base review on Home are not done yet.

items.title: Templates with derived defaults and optional parts
items.value: A parameter's default can follow another parameter, any step kind or list entry of a template can be left out by a parameter, and launchway validate expands templates from a library directory with no server.
items.detail: Defaults derive only for string parameters, from string parameters. The offline command does not know which libraries or Airfields a server allows.

groups.name: Debug a deployment, then see everything
groups.blurb: Why did it fail, in one sentence, then every resource behind it.

items.title: Why did it fail to deploy
items.value: A failed application opens with a diagnosis in one sentence, the evidence behind it and one recommended action.
items.detail: Each piece of evidence is a button that opens the resource where it shows: manifest, events or log. AI can help word the diagnosis, but the evidence is always facts. Today a failed deployment opens with a one-sentence diagnosis; the full catalog of causes grows with the Argo CD work in Milestone 8.

items.title: A timeline of changes and symptoms
items.value: Changes, new copies starting, alerts and health on a single time line, with what changed since it last worked.
items.detail: A comparison with the last working version covers image, settings and manifests.
items.needs: Why did it fail to deploy.

items.title: Everything deployed
items.value: The whole resource tree: workloads, pods, containers, services, routes, settings, volumes, jobs and custom resources.
items.detail: Each node has overview, events, manifest with desired against live, and logs. Secrets show by name only.
items.needs: Why did it fail to deploy.

items.title: Logs where you need them
items.value: Container logs now and from before the last restart, with search, follow, a time range and jump to the first error.
items.detail: Restarts, exit codes and resource use sit beside the log.

items.title: Fix actions with their consequence
items.value: Roll a setting back, retry an update or open the failing pod, each saying in words what will happen.
items.detail: Every action is a guided change that can be undone and is audited. Today the server reports which actions can work, so no button is offered that cannot.
items.needs: Why did it fail to deploy.

groups.name: Where it deploys
groups.blurb: Clusters, virtual machines, machine images, clouds and serverless.

items.title: Built-in Helm and Kubernetes deploys
items.value: Deploy and roll back without Argo CD; Argo stays first class for long-lived Airfields.
items.detail: The deploy is a typed step with a plan, a diff, health checks and a Return to base to the last good release.

items.title: Preview environments
items.value: Every pull request or branch gets its own environment and address, tested and cleaned up on merge.
items.detail: The pull request page shows the address and the verification result.

items.title: VM deploys
items.value: Roll a change across virtual machines in batches over SSH, with verification between batches.
items.detail: Hosts appear next to applications on the fleet page, with what runs on each.

items.title: Machine images with Packer
items.value: Bake machine images in a pipeline and roll them through instance groups.
items.detail: Images have contents, scan results and signatures like container images.

items.title: Image-based hosts
items.value: Machines that are really images (built on bootc), built, signed, upgraded and returned to base like container images, with host setup done at first boot.
items.detail: Staged upgrades, reboots in batches and a go-back button use the same runway as an application rollout.

items.title: First boot owned by Launchway
items.value: The first-boot unit applies host name, network, keys and zone, and may run a configuration playbook once before the host takes traffic.
items.detail: Running a playbook on a host that is already serving traffic stays refused, because that is what brings drift back.

items.title: Configuration at build time
items.value: Ansible and image builders work together at build time to prepare images.
items.detail: What belongs in the image is baked, and what must differ per host is applied at first boot.

items.title: An infrastructure stack designer
items.value: Compose image, build and configuration blocks visually and have them turned into pipelines.
items.detail: The picture and the generated files stay in step, and the result is reviewable in Git.

items.title: Image as a service for enterprise Linux teams
items.value: Watch base images and advisories, rebuild, re-sign, re-scan and roll out across zones with verification.
items.detail: You can ask whether every production host runs an approved, signed and scanned image patched inside its deadline, and get a yes or a list.

items.title: Hosts and machine images in the interface
items.value: A catalog of images with contents and base, and a hosts page showing version, staged upgrade, drift and last seen.
items.detail: A host page draws first boot as a short line, with boot history and logs.

items.title: Cloud targets: AWS, Google Cloud and Azure
items.value: Deploy to the three major clouds with their own features, with no stored cloud keys.
items.detail: Each target uses short-lived identity from the pipeline step.

items.title: Serverless and managed instance groups
items.value: Functions, container services and managed instance groups as deploy targets.
items.detail: Rollouts, health checks and Returns to base follow the same model as on Kubernetes.
items.needs: Cloud targets: AWS, Google Cloud and Azure.

groups.name: Infrastructure as code
groups.blurb: State, plans and checks you can trust.

items.title: Terraform and OpenTofu
items.value: Reviewed plans, applies that run only the reviewed plan, state kept and locked inside Launchway, and drift detection.
items.detail: Users never wonder where state goes, and Launchway guides them to good practice by default.

items.title: State and locking built in
items.value: Terraform and OpenTofu state is stored, versioned, encrypted and locked inside Launchway, with access rules.
items.detail: It speaks the standard HTTP backend, so a pipeline step needs no backend setup and existing state can be imported.

items.title: Ansible
items.value: Typed steps with per-host results and a check mode before apply.
items.detail: Results show per host, with the check result shown before anything is changed.

items.title: Chef
items.value: A real step with per-node results where Chef reports them, check mode before apply, and templates.
items.detail: Later and by choice: a real step with per-node results where Chef reports them, a check before apply, and tests as checks.

items.title: Packer builds as a first-class step
items.value: Run image builds with their results, logs and Cargo attached to the Sortie.
items.detail: Output images go to the Depot or the image store with provenance.

groups.name: Runtime configuration
groups.blurb: Settings, keys and toggles managed together, per zone and Airfield.

items.title: Feature toggles
items.value: Toggles per Airfield with rules, percentages that keep the same people, Master switches, approvals and a reason on every change, history with revert, and Go and TypeScript libraries.
items.detail: Built: the model, the safeguards, the history and revert, scheduled changes, SDK keys, the evaluation protocol with streaming and the Go and TypeScript libraries with OpenFeature providers, the toggles file, and the web, command line and agent tools. Still to come: a pipeline keyword, plans with proofs between steps, webhook events, and libraries for more languages.

items.title: Configuration, keys and toggles per zone
items.value: Manage settings and secrets together per zone and Airfield, for virtual machines and Kubernetes alike.
items.detail: A zone is a named place and failure domain such as a region or a cluster. The nearest owner wins unless a higher level has enforced the value.

items.title: Routing by client attributes
items.value: Decide which version a request gets from who sent it, such as a share of mobile clients, inside the application or at the network.
items.detail: The effective exposure of route share times toggle share is always shown.

items.title: A guided change for every lever
items.value: Preview, policy check, approval where required, applied and audited, with an undo, for toggles, weights and limits.
items.detail: Moving a lever to its safe state is never gated, and moving away from it always is.

items.title: Secrets with an external store
items.value: Read secrets from more external stores, such as the cloud providers’ own secret services. Vault, OpenBao, files and the Airfield already work.
items.detail: The store stays authoritative and values never reach the control plane.

items.title: Service mesh support including VMs
items.value: Traffic, identity and policy for services on a mesh, and for virtual machines that join it.
items.detail: Machines outside the mesh still appear on the map as declared.

groups.name: Watch and protect
groups.blurb: See traffic, protect it, and know whether each service is meeting its target.

items.title: A live traffic map
items.value: See how traffic flows between services, workloads and virtual machines, with rates, errors and latency.
items.detail: Each connection says whether it was observed, declared or not observed, and no number is ever made up for one that is not observed.

items.title: Diagnose along a flow
items.value: From a red connection, a one-sentence diagnosis, the failing requests, the pod, the change that caused it and the logs.
items.detail: You go from symptom to cause without changing tools.

items.title: Replay the last hours
items.value: A time slider that replays the last twelve hours of the map with incidents and rollouts marked.
items.detail: Useful for what changed when errors began.

items.title: Inject delays and errors safely
items.value: Add a delay or an error to a share of requests on a healthy connection, with a hard limit on share and time.
items.detail: The dialog shows who is affected, and conditions stop the test early.

items.title: Rate limiting and traffic protection
items.value: Limits per client, route and customer, connection limits, timeouts, retries and circuit breakers, shown with how close traffic is to each.
items.detail: Changing one is a guided change with a preview that replays the last hour against the new value.

items.title: Attack and abuse signals
items.value: Signs of attack or abuse as plain sentences with evidence and three actions: limit, block or ignore with a reason.
items.detail: Each signal says honestly where it came from.

items.title: Reliability pages
items.value: Services ranked by error budget, saturation and restarts, with deploys, settings, toggles and scaling marked on the charts.
items.detail: Cause and effect are visible on one time line.

items.title: Toggles in context
items.value: Which features are on where and for whom, with the effect of a toggle shown and one button to turn it off.
items.detail: Toggle first, roll back second, in seconds.

items.title: Signal sources
items.value: Connect metrics, logs, analytics, traces, the mesh, a firewall and the toggle service, with a test for each.
items.detail: Every chart names its source and links to the query.

items.title: Service reliability targets
items.value: Set targets for the services you run and see whether a release is spending the budget.
items.detail: Targets can be imported and exported in an open format.

groups.name: Change and insight
groups.blurb: Know what changed, who approved it, and how delivery is going.

items.title: Change management
items.value: Automatic change records with risk scores, freezes and approvals, and optional two-way sync with an IT service tool.
items.detail: Works standalone, so a team without such a tool still has records.

items.title: Connections to ServiceNow and Jira Service Management
items.value: Create and update change records in ServiceNow or Jira Service Management and take their approval back.
items.detail: Optional and equal to the built-in records.

items.title: Delivery metrics and executive dashboards
items.value: Deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate and time to restore, with drill-down to the Sorties behind each number.
items.detail: Graphs are meant for people who do not use Launchway daily.

items.title: Test intelligence and flow insights
items.value: Find slow and flaky tests, bottlenecks in review and idle time in delivery.
items.detail: Suggestions are shown with the evidence.

items.title: Policy rules in an open language
items.value: Write extra policy rules in an open policy language alongside the built-in rules.
items.detail: Rules run at the same decision point and are shown in the verdict.

items.title: Portfolio bill of materials
items.value: A bill of materials across every image as well as every project, with export. Searching components across projects already works.
items.detail: Pairs with the software graph.

items.title: Experiments with toggles
items.value: Compare outcomes between users with a toggle on and off.
items.detail: Results join delivery data, so you see effect and cost.

groups.name: Moving over from other delivery platforms
groups.blurb: Importers and proof for teams that already have a delivery platform.

items.title: Importers for other delivery platforms
items.value: Convert pipelines, services and Airfields from other delivery and GitOps platforms, with a report of what needs a person.
items.detail: The report is honest about gaps.

items.title: Published proof points
items.value: Measured comparisons of footprint, speed and capabilities that anyone can reproduce.
items.detail: Methods and results are published.

items.title: Enterprise readiness checklist
items.value: Answers to the questions an enterprise reviewer asks, with a support bundle and an evidence page.
items.detail: Close the gaps that gate adoption.

groups.name: The golden path
groups.blurb: A developer describes what an application is in a short file, or in nothing at all; the platform team says how things are delivered once; Launchway does the rest and records the evidence.

items.title: A small workload description
items.value: A short file in the repository says what an application is: how it listens, its health check, its backing services and the names of its secrets.
items.detail: Detection can fill it in. Launchway derives the pipeline, checks and rollout plan from it.

items.title: Import from and export to Score
items.value: The workload description reads and writes the open Score specification, so you are never locked in.
items.detail: First landing: Kubernetes with Argo CD.

items.title: Landings chosen per environment
items.value: The platform team chooses where each Airfield lands, and the same description is delivered there.
items.detail: Kubernetes first.

items.title: Virtual machine and bootable-container landings
items.value: The same description can land as a package or machine image on virtual machines, or on a fleet of bootable-container hosts.
items.detail: Second phase.

items.title: Serverless and managed container landings
items.value: The same description can land as a function or a managed container service.
items.detail: Later phase.

items.title: Show what was generated, and eject
items.value: Everything Launchway generates can be shown, and a team can take ownership of the generated files for one landing.
items.detail: Never a black box and never a silent rewrite of your repository.

items.title: Automatic change records
items.value: Every delivery becomes a change record with its evidence, without anyone filling in a form.
items.detail: Facts come from the pipeline, the proofs and the approvals.

items.title: Standard, normal and emergency changes
items.value: A repeatable low-risk change is approved by a rule; a normal change goes to the right people with the evidence; an emergency change acts first and is reviewed after.
items.detail: Risk is computed from facts and shown with its reasoning.

items.title: Separation of duties
items.value: The author of a change is never its only approver, and nobody approves a rule that applies to them.
items.detail: An unavailable action says why.

items.title: Freezes and a release calendar
items.value: A hold blocks approval and the production step for a time, while work continues up to it, and a calendar shows windows and scheduled changes.
items.detail: Emergency changes use their own path.

items.title: An external change system, optional
items.value: Change records can be sent to and approved in an external change management system through an adapter.
items.detail: The built-in changes area works with no adapter.

items.title: A security review only when the facts warrant it
items.value: A lightweight review is triggered by facts such as a new public route or a new kind of data, not on every change.
items.detail: Continuous checks run on every change regardless.

items.title: Golden path health for the platform team
items.value: See how many deliveries follow the path, where developers leave it and which standard stops the most.
items.detail: A view for the platform owner.

groups.name: Built-in platform services
groups.blurb: Four things that sit next to your pipelines are built in and optional: object storage, Terraform and OpenTofu state, a managed cache and Switches. Each can be swapped for the product you already run.

items.title: S3-compatible object storage
items.value: A small S3-compatible front door on the storage Launchway already has, speaking the part of S3 that Terraform, Depots, backup tools and build caches use.
items.detail: Promised for Launchway’s own data and your pipelines. For production application data you connect your own bucket, or bundle a managed server.

items.title: Short-lived storage credentials
items.value: A step proves its identity and gets a temporary key, so a pipeline never holds a stored storage key.
items.detail: Part of the first phase.

items.title: Versioning, lifecycle and events for storage
items.value: Keep versions, expire objects by rule and send events when objects change.
items.detail: Second phase.

items.title: State you can read safely
items.value: Terraform and OpenTofu state is shown as a difference with secrets masked and never as raw text, with history and Return to base.
items.detail: Second phase, after state and locking.

items.title: A managed cache as a backing service
items.value: Give an application a cache in an Airfield: a managed Valkey, installed through GitOps, with its credentials in the vault.
items.detail: Launchway is not a database vendor, and says so. PostgreSQL covers Launchway’s own needs.

items.title: Give this app a backing service
items.value: The same pattern provisions a cache, a database, a Holding pattern or object storage for an application and wires it in as a connection.
items.detail: Third phase.

items.title: Toggle providers for the main languages
items.value: Thin OpenFeature providers for Go, Java, JavaScript and TypeScript, Python and .NET read toggles from Launchway.
items.detail: Rules evaluate inside the application, so personal data never leaves it.

items.title: Toggles keep working when Launchway is down
items.value: Providers keep the last known values and verify signed rules, so an outage never flips a feature.
items.detail: Also evaluation counts for hygiene.

items.title: Bring your own backend
items.value: Each platform service has a built-in default and a popular backend you can use instead, without losing data.
items.detail: What you install: Launchway, and PostgreSQL for production.

groups.name: Configuration as code and the automation control center
groups.blurb: Everything that configures a system is code in Git, reviewed like code, applied from a plan, and watched for drift.

items.title: A configuration change is a plan
items.value: A dry run is its first proof, people give go or no-go on the reviewed plan, Launchway applies exactly what was reviewed, and the way back is the previous version.
items.detail: Ansible cannot apply a saved plan the way Terraform can, so a guard enforces it and the page says so.

items.title: Inventories
items.value: Hosts come from a static list first, then from clusters, clouds and other sources, with search over what is known about each.
items.detail: Inventory stays on your side on the hosted service.

items.title: Flight plans as job templates, with a form
items.value: A stack or playbook becomes a Flight plan with a form for its inputs, a schedule, credentials and role-based access.
items.detail: A wizard writes the pipeline for a repository it finds.

items.title: Results for every host
items.value: See per host and per task what changed, with the tool’s own output kept alongside.
items.detail: Launchway keeps the tool’s own output beside a readable summary.

items.title: Drift and converge now
items.value: See which hosts and resources differ from their code and why, and press converge with the same clearance as any change.
items.detail: Drift is checked on a schedule and shown per host.

items.title: Short-lived access to hosts
items.value: Runs use workload identity or per-run secure shell certificates, never a stored cloud key.
items.detail: Least privilege for hosts and secrets.

items.title: Launchway’s own settings as code, both ways
items.value: Change settings on screen or in Git; each way produces a visible, reviewable change in the other.
items.detail: Built on the Terraform provider.

items.title: Event-driven fixes
items.value: An alert or a drift report can start a reviewed fix, with limits so it cannot run away.
items.detail: Second phase.

items.title: Other configuration tools later
items.value: Agent-based tools and other infrastructure tools join through one common interface.
items.detail: Third phase.

You promote the exact image tested in staging to production with no copy.
Retention cleans old images but keeps the one a cluster is running.
A project's packages tab shows its images and charts and where each runs.

groups.name: The registry
groups.blurb: Images, charts and other Cargo stored beside the code, under the same permissions.

items.title: A built-in OCI registry
items.value: Store container images, Helm charts and other OCI Cargo in Launchway, with nothing else to run. First slice built: the Distribution API under /v2/ (chunked and resumable uploads that work across servers, cross-repository mounts, Range reads, referrers, multi-platform indexes), private by default, in the same database and blob store as everything else.

items.title: Helm charts and other artifacts as first-class
items.value: Charts, signatures, bills of materials, attestations, operating-system images and WebAssembly modules are stored and shown properly.
items.detail: Charts and any OCI Cargo are stored, listed with their type and fetched with helm; signatures, SBOMs and scan results are attached as referrers and shown. Not yet: a chart page with its versions, which applications use it and the values it accepts.

items.title: An image page that tells the whole story
items.value: Where an image runs now, tags, layers, vulnerabilities with fixes, contents, signature, provenance and the Sortie and commit that built it.
items.detail: The Depot tab of Images lists repositories, tags and manifests with size, digest, platforms, who pushed each from which run, whether it is signed, has an SBOM, a vulnerability summary and a pull reference to copy. Not yet: where it runs now, layers, and the history drawn as a line.

items.title: Promotion by digest
items.value: Move an image from one Airfield to the next without copying or rebuilding it.
items.detail: What was tested is exactly what ships.

items.title: Retention that protects what runs
items.value: Clean up old images without ever deleting one that is deployed.
items.detail: Retention rules (keep the newest N, keep tags matching patterns, untagged older than D days) at installation, project and repository level, with an exact preview before anything is deleted; an image an Airfield runs is never deleted, by retention or by hand. Cleanup is mark and sweep with a grace period, safe beside pushes. The label saying why each item is kept is not built.

items.title: Policy on push and deploy
items.value: The same policy engine checks an image when it is pushed to the built-in Depot, as it already does for a push from a pipeline and for a deploy.
items.detail: Unsigned, unscanned or vulnerable images can be refused at either point.

items.title: Pull-through cache
items.value: Cache public images and packages so builds are faster, work offline, and never serve an out-of-date copy of something that can change.
items.detail: Cached images are scanned and counted against quotas like any other.

items.title: Image guard for sandboxed builds
items.value: Keep unchecked images away from sandboxed builds, and fetch every image through a checking proxy.
items.detail: Names that resolve to private addresses are refused.

items.title: Replication with other registries
items.value: Copy images to and from other registries on a rule.
items.detail: Useful for a disaster-recovery copy or a customer-facing mirror.

items.title: Per-project packages and permissions
items.value: A packages tab in each project that is a filtered view of the Depot, with per-package access.
items.detail: Every repository belongs to the project named by its first path component and follows the project's roles (viewer pulls, operator pushes, admin deletes); the Depot tab shows a project's repositories. Per-package access inside a project is not built.

items.title: Signing and verification
items.value: Sign images on build and verify signatures on pull and deploy.
items.detail: Signatures and attestations an image step writes are stored next to the image and shown. Verifying signatures on pull and deploy is not built.

items.title: More package formats
items.value: Language and system packages, such as for common programming languages, with cleanup rules and quotas.
items.detail: Added in order of demand, with a shared storage model.

items.title: Any other registry, equally
items.value: Pushing to any OCI registry works today and stays first class beside the built-in one.
items.detail: Choose per project and move later.

items.title: Pipelines that build, test and publish only
items.value: Not everything deploys: a pipeline for a library, command-line tool, image or chart ends at published and available.
items.detail: The Sortie page says what was published and who uses it.

items.title: Native endpoints for package clients
items.value: Go and npm clients talk to Launchway directly, and Python, Maven, NuGet, Cargo and RubyGems follow.
items.detail: Short-lived credentials are wired in, so no stored token is needed.

items.title: Who uses which version
items.value: A library page shows which projects fetched which version and which are behind.
items.detail: Comes from publish and fetch records.

milestones.name: The software graph, with automated patching
milestones.promise: One connected picture of code, dependencies, images and deployments, so you always know what runs where and can fix it safely.
milestones.audience: Teams and security groups who need to know what runs where, what it is made of and how to fix it safely.
milestones.what: Milestone 5 connects code, dependencies, images and deployments in one graph kept in Launchway's own database. It answers what is running, from what, containing what and is any of it vulnerable. Patching then becomes an ordinary change that goes through tests, change management and a controlled rollout.
scenarios: A new advisory arrives; Launchway lists the services affected and who owns each.
You search for a function across every repository you can see.
Automatic patching is switched on for one zone; a Maintenance arrives as a change, passes its tests and rolls out.
An agent asks which services use a library and gets an answer from the graph, not from reading files.

flowchart TD Code["Code and commits"] --> Graph[("Software graph")] Deps["Packages and licenses"] --> Graph Img["Images and charts"] --> Graph Dep["Deployments and hosts"] --> Graph Adv["Advisories"] --> Graph Graph --> Q["Questions
what, where, who, how bad"] Graph --> Patch["Patch proposal"] Patch --> Review["Tests and change management"] Review --> Roll["Rollout and verification"] Roll --> Dep
milestones.diagramNote: The graph is built from facts Launchway already records, keyed by what is deployed.
done: For any running image Launchway can show its commit, run, components and findings.
A new advisory re-scores running software without a rebuild.
An automated patch reaches production only through the same gates as any change.
Patching can be switched off per zone and is off by default.
notIncluded: Cost management and the developer portal (Beyond).

groups.name: Know what you run
groups.blurb: One connected picture of code, dependencies, images and deployments.

items.title: Findings and SBOMs per run
items.value: The starting point already works: findings and components recorded for every Sortie.
items.detail: Components are recorded as bills of materials and findings are kept with the Sortie.

items.title: What is deployed where
items.value: Link every deployed image back to its commit, its components and its findings, including on hosts Launchway only observes.
items.detail: Facts are keyed by image digest and by deployment, so one query can answer across Git, the Depot, scans and the deploy engine.

items.title: A continuous observer of what runs
items.value: Watch clusters and hosts for what is actually running, not only what was deployed.
items.detail: Surprises, such as an image nobody deployed, are flagged.

items.title: Continuous scanning of what runs
items.value: Scan deployed software for new vulnerabilities and best-practice gaps, not only at build time.
items.detail: A new advisory re-scores everything already running.

items.title: Advisories, exceptions and licenses
items.value: Record which vulnerabilities apply, import vendor statements that they do not, and check licenses.
items.detail: A finding can be waived with a reason and an expiry.

items.title: Who owns what
items.value: Each component, service and repository has an owner, and findings go to that owner.
items.detail: Questions like which services use this library get an answer.

items.title: Code search across repositories
items.value: Search symbols and text across every repository, hosted or connected, filtered by what you may see.
items.detail: Results include pipelines, templates and steps.

items.title: Code intelligence
items.value: Definitions, references and call information, for people and for agents.
items.detail: Gives agents the context they need without sending whole repositories.

items.title: Code knowledge for AI, with fewer tokens
items.value: Answer AI questions from a graph of code and deployments instead of pasting files.
items.detail: Fewer tokens are sent and the answers cite where they came from.

items.title: Blast radius of a vulnerability
items.value: From an advisory, see which deployed services and Airfields are affected and who owns them.
items.detail: The list becomes a set of proposed fixes.

groups.name: Fix it safely
groups.blurb: Patch as a normal change, with checks and a controlled rollout.

items.title: Automated patching
items.value: Off by default and turned on per zone: updates open as changes, pass tests and change management, and roll out through Argo CD.
items.detail: The loop is propose, test, approve, roll out and verify, and every step is recorded.

items.title: Built-in dependency updates
items.value: Launchway finds outdated and vulnerable dependencies in a repository and proposes the updates as ordinary reviewable pull requests, so no outside update robot is needed.
items.detail: Available for Go modules, npm, Python manifests, container base images, and the workflow files a repository still carries. Known vulnerabilities are matched against OSV data (a mirror directory works offline), security fixes come first and are not held back, other versions wait three days after release, and a limit keeps a burst of pull requests from flooding the pipeline. Lock files are written by the ecosystem's own tool in a step container, never on the server. Launchway's own repository uses it. Coming, not available yet: Maven and Gradle, Cargo, .NET, Helm charts and Terraform providers; changelog excerpts in the pull request; settings edited in the web interface (today they are the repository's file and the levels' settings); automatic merging.
items.needs: Pull requests on the built-in host.

items.title: Lock files regenerated in a container and checked
items.value: When an update changes a dependency, the lock file is rebuilt in an isolated container and the result is verified before the pull request is opened.
items.detail: Built and tested, in final integration. The container has no secrets and no route to your network, so an update cannot reach anything it should not.

items.title: Image refresh and patching of base images
items.value: Rebuild images when their base changes and roll the new ones out.
items.detail: Fits into the same patching loop and its deadlines.

items.title: AI-proposed fixes
items.value: An optional helper proposes a fix or an upgrade note, flagged as AI, never merged on its own.
items.detail: A person approves, and everything it did is recorded.

items.title: Patch deadlines and evidence
items.value: Track how long each vulnerability has been open and produce evidence of patching within your own deadline.
items.detail: The question is every production host patched in time answered with a query.

groups.name: Build and release in dependency order
groups.blurb: Launchway works the order out from what your code says and shows how it knew; you can always correct it.

items.title: One dependency graph, with where each link came from
items.value: Every link says where it was found, how sure Launchway is and offers the fix right there: add a link, ignore a wrong one with a reason.
items.detail: Built on the software graph, not a second graph.

items.title: Libraries first, then what uses them
items.value: When a library changes it is built and published first, and each application that uses it is built after, once, in order.
items.detail: Go, npm, Maven, Gradle, Python and base images first.

items.title: Dependents checked before a change merges
items.value: A library’s pull request builds the applications that use it against the new version and reports the result.
items.detail: The result appears on the library’s pull request as a check.

items.title: Limits on build storms
items.value: Batching and caps keep one library change from starting a flood of dependent builds.
items.detail: A person can pause or reorder.

items.title: Order you can override
items.value: Set build and release order by hand, pin a version, and mark an edge wrong; the system works out the order and a person can always override.
items.detail: Overrides are kept in the repository or in settings.

items.title: Formations: things that go together
items.value: A Formation is a release unit of applications, databases and configuration that are delivered together in the right order.
items.detail: No new kind of object: a Formation is a plan with members.

items.title: One go or no-go, one watch, one way back
items.value: A Formation has one decision, one timeline and one watch, and returns to the stable state in reverse order.
items.detail: If part of a Formation fails, the others return to the stable state.

items.title: Database first, then the application
items.value: A Formation expands the database first, deploys services in dependency order and finishes the contract step later.
items.detail: Builds on database change delivery.

items.title: Linked changes across repositories
items.value: One change that spans several repositories is tracked, tested and merged together.
items.detail: Second phase.

items.title: Branching patterns as Flight plans
items.value: Trunk-based, short-lived branches with pull requests, the long-lived develop-and-release flow, release branches, tag-based library releases, forks, pull-request promotion and monorepos each come as a Flight plan.
items.detail: Each says what it implies for branches, triggers, versions, Airfields and fixes.

items.title: A recommender for the branching pattern
items.value: When a repository is created or imported, six plain questions lead to the simplest pattern that fits, with the reason and the trade-offs, set up in one step.
items.detail: Help, never enforcement.

milestones.name: AI as an optional first-class helper
milestones.promise: AI wherever it saves effort, always optional, always off until an administrator turns a purpose on, and never able to hide a failure.
milestones.audience: Anyone who wants AI help with delivery, and anyone who wants it kept out.
milestones.what: Milestone 6 puts AI wherever it saves effort and keeps it entirely optional. A built-in gateway routes to any model with spending limits, local models are first-class, regulated projects have a protected path, and a failing check can never be hidden by a model.

A regulated project is allowed to use only models with recorded data terms.
A step calls the gateway by model name; moving to another provider needs no pipeline change.
You sketch a delivery and are shown a pipeline you can read and edit.

groups.name: Today
groups.blurb: What already works.

items.title: Models in steps and verification

items.title: Agents as users

items.title: A built-in model gateway

items.title: Local and self-hosted models

items.title: Provider switching and fallbacks

items.detail: No code changes in pipelines.

items.title: Usage monitoring
items.value: See usage by model, project and purpose, with cost.
items.detail: Charts feed the same dashboards as everything else.

items.title: Spending limits
items.value: Budgets in money, per model, project and purpose, not only in tokens.
items.detail: Calls stop or warn when a limit is reached.

items.title: From a picture to a pipeline

milestones.name: The hosted service, the public demo and enterprise controls
milestones.promise: Sign up and go, or keep your files on your own machines; hosted, hosted with your own machines, or self-hosted, with easy moves between them, and a wall around every customer’s Base.
milestones.audience: Start-ups, freelancers and small teams first, then enterprises and regulated teams that must keep everything on their side.
milestones.what: Milestone 7 lets you use Launchway without running it, and shows people the way to run it themselves when that suits them better. The first customers are small teams, so sign-up is short: an email or an existing account, a strong second factor, and a guided first project. Three ways to run it share one product: fully hosted, hosted with your own machines doing the work and holding the files, or self-hosted, and a team can move between them one project or one Base at a time. The hosted service is protected from its customers and its customers from it and from each other, and it is never a place to park files. It opens to outsiders in stages, each only after its checks pass. Plans have every feature on; what changes is a limit, and the spend limit starts at zero. The same milestone adds the identity, audit and retention controls enterprises ask for.
scenarios: Two friends at two houses sign up, protect their accounts with a passkey, and have a first green build in minutes, with no network set-up on either side.
A team that does not want its files on anyone else’s server chooses to keep them on its own machines, and both people reach them through Launchway over an encrypted relay that cannot read them.
A team that started fully hosted moves one project to its own hardware with a preview first, and keeps working during the move.
A Base nearing the hosted size limit gets plain notices and a guided move, and is never locked out of its own data.
A regulated team enables encryption keys with rotation and a retention rule.
An auditor exports a tamper-evident audit trail to the security tools.
A visitor explores the public demo with realistic data.

deepDives.title: The hosted service and sandboxed runners

groups.name: Hosted service and demo
groups.blurb: Use Launchway without running it, on a plan that follows your choices.

items.title: Hosted service
items.value: Launchway as a service: sign-up, quotas, usage metering, a free plan with every feature on, pay for use, and data residency.
items.detail: Price follows your choices, such as availability and users, and no feature is held back by plan.

items.title: Free tier and pay for use
items.value: A free tier, and pay-for-use billing from the start, with no extras for basics.
items.detail: Usage is metered and shown before it is billed, and the spend limit starts at zero. Prices and limits are not decided yet.

items.title: Data residency
items.value: Choose where your data lives.
items.detail: Region choices are shown at sign-up and recorded.

items.title: Runners on your machines
items.value: Stations on your own servers or clusters connect out to the hosted engine, so code and secrets never leave your network.
items.detail: Only outbound connections are needed, and the same Station command works from a laptop. Builds are placed across a team’s machines as described in Milestone 2.

items.title: Sandboxed hosted runners
items.value: Each step in its own isolated machine, with no route to anything but the internet and firm quotas; the same profile available to any self-hosted server.
items.detail: Layers of isolation back each other up, and a Master switch exists at the network.

items.title: Hosted capacity that can grow
items.value: Everything is portable, so capacity can be added on any provider as demand justifies.
items.detail: Nothing is tied to one machine.

items.title: A public demo
items.value: A safe instance on the internet with realistic data anyone can explore, read-only at first. A local demo already runs from the quick start.
items.detail: Try it with your own Station follows once Wing isolation exists.

items.title: Several Wings on one Base
items.value: Several Wings on one installation, isolated from each other, with the level names you choose.
items.detail: Isolation is tested.

groups.name: Sign up and go
groups.blurb: The first customers are start-ups, freelancers and small teams, so the front door is short and safe.

items.title: Sign up with the least set-up
items.value: One front door where anyone signs up with an email address or an existing account, proves the address, protects the account, names their Base and lands in a guided first project.
items.detail: The aim is a first green build in minutes. The same sentence is shown whether or not an address is already known, so the form reveals nothing about who has an account.

items.title: Passkeys, authenticator apps and recovery codes
items.value: The account is bound to something only its owner has: a passkey, preferably, or an authenticator app, with recovery codes shown once. The owner and every administrator must use one of the strong ones.
items.detail: Text-message codes are not offered on purpose, because they can be taken over. An email code proves an address; it is never treated as a second factor for owners.

items.title: Recovery that is not a back door
items.value: A lost second factor is recovered through the other factors you set up, or through a waiting period with notices to every session and to the account’s email.
items.detail: Staff cannot reset a second factor or let anyone in, so no one can talk their way past it.
items.needs: Passkeys, authenticator apps and recovery codes.

items.title: Sign-up protection that respects privacy
items.value: Rate limits, a small puzzle the browser solves and friction for throwaway addresses guard the form, with no tracking, no outside challenge service and no phone numbers.
items.detail: Behavior after sign-up is judged on what an account does, not who it is.

items.title: A guided first project
items.value: Pick a starter, create or import a repository, push or edit in the browser, see a green build, and invite a teammate with one link.
items.detail: Everything is optional later: your own secrets manager, Depot, Stations and identity provider are offered with a wizard, never required.
items.needs: A built-in starter library for each language.

items.title: Protected both ways
items.value: The service is protected from its customers’ code and content, and customers are protected from the operator and from each other.
items.detail: Each protection has a mechanism and a test; the operator sees counts and health, never content.

items.title: Leave completely
items.value: Export a whole Base in an open format, then delete it: after a grace period its keys are destroyed, which makes every copy, including backups, unreadable, and a certificate says so.
items.detail: The export imports into a self-hosted installation, so leaving is a move, not a loss.

groups.name: Three ways to run, and easy moves between them
groups.blurb: One product, three places to keep your work. Choose at sign-up, change your mind later, and nothing is held hostage.

items.title: Fully hosted
items.value: The default: repositories, pipelines, Stations, secrets, Depot and reports all on the hosted service, with nothing to install.
items.detail: The honest trade is stated at sign-up: the service stores your code and secrets, in your own Base, encrypted, walled off and never readable by the vendor console.
items.needs: Every customer has its own Base.

items.title: Hosted with your own Detachment
items.value: The hosted screens and coordination, with builds, secrets and deployments on your side.
items.detail: A project can move here one at a time. The Detachment only calls out, so no port is opened and no tunnel is needed.

items.title: Files on your own machines, through a sealed relay
items.value: Two people, two houses, no hosted copies: each runs one command, and both reach the files through Launchway over an end-to-end encrypted session that the relay carries but cannot read.
items.detail: The hosted side keeps only accounts, who is on the team, which machines are online and opaque identifiers, never a file name, commit or log. No address, tunnel or certificate is set up at either end.

items.title: Replicas across two machines
items.value: With two machines, every repository has a full copy on each, pushes go to whichever is reachable, and they catch up with each other when both are online.
items.detail: Protected branches have one home at a time, a true disagreement is kept visible and never overwritten, and the product prints the honest limits, such as a sleeping laptop.
items.needs: Files on your own machines, through a sealed relay.

items.title: Backup and recovery on your own machines
items.value: The second machine is a live copy, and an optional encrypted backup goes to storage you own, with a walk-through for “my laptop died”.
items.detail: The hosted service says plainly that it cannot restore what it never held.

items.title: Self-hosted, the same product
items.value: Everything on your own machines, installed with the guided installer, with the same features and the same export format.
items.detail: Nothing about the hosted service is needed to run it.

items.title: Guided moves between the three
items.value: Move one project or a whole Base, in either direction, from a button or one command, after a preview that lists what will move and what you must decide.
items.detail: A move mirrors first, verifies every reference and object, switches in seconds, keeps the old address redirecting and offers a Return to base window before the source is deleted.

items.title: Secrets move without being exposed
items.value: Secret values are re-sealed to the destination’s key, exported under a passphrase only you know, or re-entered and rotated, so they are never in the clear on the way.
items.detail: You choose the way in the preview.

groups.name: A size ceiling, with notices, and nothing held hostage
groups.blurb: Hosting is for teams that fit; the ones that outgrow it are helped on, never locked out.

items.title: Size ceilings on hosted Bases
items.value: Each hosted Base has a ceiling. As it approaches, Launchway says what is growing, offers cleanup and offers the guided move, and at the ceiling only the growing kind of data stops.
items.detail: Reading, cloning, downloading, exporting and moving always keep working, builds on your own Stations keep running, and data is never deleted for being over a ceiling. The limits themselves are not decided yet.

items.title: Nothing held hostage
items.value: Every hosted Base can be exported completely, at any time, in an open and documented format with a verifier.
items.detail: The export, the move and deletion are tested on every release, including the round trip back.

groups.name: Never a place to park files
groups.blurb: The hosted service is for your work, not for storing arbitrary files, and it is built so it cannot become that.

items.title: Nothing anonymous or public
items.value: No repository, Cargo, image, page, report or file on the hosted service can be reached without signing in as a member of that Base.
items.detail: There are no public project pages, no hosted sites and no direct download addresses. Share links are absent at first.

items.title: No general file storage
items.value: The service holds repositories, build results and Depot images that pipelines produce, and nothing else: there is no upload-a-file feature.
items.detail: Per-file, per-push and total quotas, short retention for build results and upload rate limits keep even that small and bounded.

items.title: Identity checks in proportion to risk
items.value: A verified address, a second factor and limits that start low for a new account and rise as it shows normal use.
items.detail: Throwaway addresses add a cool-down rather than a refusal.

items.title: Abuse reports, takedown and suspension
items.value: A published way to report abuse, a process to act on it, suspension with an appeal, and detection that respects the promise that the operator cannot read your work.
items.detail: Known-bad material and unusual behavior can be noticed without reading customers’ content.

items.title: Customer files kept apart from the operator’s own systems
items.value: Whatever outsiders store is kept on capacity separate from anything the operator runs for itself, with its own keys per Base.
items.detail: Where that capacity is rented is a decision still to be made and announced.

groups.name: Opening in stages
groups.blurb: Outsiders are let in a step at a time, and a step opens only when every check for it and for the earlier ones is green.

items.title: Stage 1: invited people
items.value: A handful of people the operator knows use the hosted service under a short plain agreement, with their own Stations.
items.detail: No customer code runs on the service at this stage.
items.needs: Proven by tests that gate every release.

items.title: Stage 2: files on your own machines
items.value: The first public opening offers only the mode where files stay on your machines. Fully hosted is shown as coming, never as a choice that fails.
items.detail: It needs no customer storage, no content scanning and no Station isolation, so it can open first. An independent penetration test is required before it does.
items.needs: Files on your own machines, through a sealed relay.

items.title: Stage 3: fully hosted, on rented capacity
items.value: Public sign-up with hosted storage, your own Stations and takedown tools, on capacity rented for the purpose.
items.detail: It requires the wall between Bases, the abuse process, the size ceilings and a second independent test.
items.needs: Never a place to park files.

items.title: Stage 4: hosted runners
items.value: Public sign-up with sandboxed Stations run by the service.
items.detail: It requires the Station isolation suite, a test that tries to escape, and abuse limits on compute.

groups.name: Plans that follow your choices
groups.blurb: A free plan with every feature, and no surprises on the bill.

items.title: Every feature on, the spend limit at zero
items.value: The free plan turns every feature on. A plan changes limits, never features, and a new account’s spend limit starts at zero, so nothing can be charged until its owner raises it.
items.detail: Prices and numeric limits are not decided and are not published here.

groups.name: A hosted service that never holds your network or secrets
groups.blurb: Before the first outside customer. The hosted side coordinates; a small program on your side, the Detachment, does the work.

items.title: The Detachment
items.value: One small program on your side starts your Stations, looks things up in your secret store and reads your clusters, metrics, logs and DNS.
items.detail: It only calls out; nothing is opened into your network. It holds your secrets, reaches your systems and sees your traffic, so the hosted side never does.

items.title: The boundary, data kind by data kind
items.value: A published table says what stays with you, what crosses and what the hosted side may see, such as names, states, counts and timings.
items.detail: Secrets, traffic, logs and code never cross by default.

items.title: Screens drawn from your data, not stored hosted
items.value: The pages you read are drawn in your browser from data fetched live from your Detachment over an encrypted channel.
items.detail: Even the operator of the hosted service cannot see your traffic.

items.title: Your logs, artifacts and audit stay with you
items.value: Build logs, Debriefs, Cargo and an audit trail you own are kept on your side by default; storing them hosted is a per-Wing choice with a key you hold.
items.detail: The hosted service keeps a separate record of what it did.

items.title: Least privilege grants
items.value: You grant access to your systems from none upward, each step showing what it adds.
items.detail: Monitoring data is a permission, never a raw pass-through.

items.title: Updates you control
items.value: Signed updates with a pin, a window and a Return to base; your Detachment checks the signature and your policy before accepting.
items.detail: The hosted side cannot make it run new code.

items.title: Works when the hosted service is unreachable
items.value: Your Detachment keeps working for what it can, then catches up.
items.detail: Your Sorties are not hostage to an outage.

items.title: Verify the promise yourself
items.value: Ways to check the boundary: the wire format is closed, a Pathfinder test shows nothing leaks, and you can inspect what the Detachment sends.
items.detail: Staff cannot read anything stored hosted without your approved, time-limited session.
items.needs: The boundary, data kind by data kind.

items.title: Self-hosted is the same shape
items.value: The same Detachment serves a self-hosted installation, so moving between them is a configuration change.
items.detail: Leaving is complete: export, move, destroy the hosted copy with a recorded key destruction.

items.title: Air-gapped and restricted networks
items.value: An offline bundle and a customer-run relay for networks with no outside access.
items.detail: It later includes the interface served by your own Detachment.

groups.name: A protected demonstration
groups.blurb: Before the first outside visitor. Anyone can try every feature while the operator’s systems stay protected.

items.title: A demonstration world
items.value: A visitor gets sample repositories, a simulated cluster and metrics, a rollout, a failing deployment and a moving traffic map, with nothing real behind them.
items.detail: It is built from the same fixtures the product’s own tests use.

items.title: Isolated by construction
items.value: The demonstration runs apart from everything else, runs no code a visitor brings, and has a Master switch.
items.detail: A visitor never gets sight of the operator’s own network.

items.title: Easy to try, hard to abuse
items.value: Sign-up is quick, with limits and cost guards against misuse.
items.detail: A visitor can connect their own Detachment later.

items.title: The whole product, safely
items.value: DNS, chaos, databases, virtual machines and the edge fill in after the first world, each as a fixture with a conformance test.
items.detail: Every feature can be seen without risk.

groups.name: Identity, audit and compliance
groups.blurb: The controls enterprises and regulated teams ask for.

items.title: Built-in accounts with MFA
items.value: Small teams without an identity provider still get secure sign-in with authenticator codes or passkeys.
items.detail: Built: accounts with Argon2id password hashes, a password policy with an offline blocklist, sign-in rate limits with lockout and backoff, authenticator codes (TOTP) with recovery codes, required for administrators by default, a one-time setup code for the first administrator, invitations and resets by one-time link or by the console command launchway users reset, sessions with idle and absolute limits and sign out everywhere, and an audit entry for every sign-in event. Not built yet: passkeys (WebAuthn) and outgoing mail.

items.title: Directory groups and custom roles
items.value: LDAP and Active Directory groups mapped to roles at each level, leavers removed automatically, and a view of who can do what, and why.
items.detail: Roles are custom and permissions are clear.

items.title: Other single sign-on and provisioning
items.value: SAML sign-in and automatic user provisioning for larger companies.
items.detail: Works beside directory groups.

items.title: Tamper-evident audit and SIEM export
items.value: An audit trail nobody can quietly edit, streamed to your security tools.
items.detail: Entries are chained so a gap shows.

items.title: Retention, legal hold and encryption at rest
items.value: Choose how long data is kept, prove deletion, and encrypt logs and Cargo with rotating keys; encrypted by default when hosted.
items.detail: A hold overrides cleanup. Encryption at rest with a key held outside the database is being built now (see Milestone 12).

items.title: A compliance pack for PCI DSS and HIPAA
items.value: Policy templates and an evidence report that maps controls to requirements. It supports your compliance work and is not a certification.
items.detail: Controls are listed with evidence.

items.title: Zero trust throughout
items.value: Every service, Station and person proves identity on every call.
items.detail: No shared secrets between components.

groups.name: Your own Base, and what the service sees
groups.blurb: On the hosted product every customer has its own complete Base. The service operator sees the service, never your work, and you choose what to send when you need help.

items.title: Every customer has its own Base
items.value: A customer’s top level is its own complete, private Base, and the highest thing that customer can see or name.
items.detail: Inside it the usual levels apply.

items.title: The operator’s own Base is walled off
items.value: The service operator’s own Base is a separate Base that no customer or demonstration visitor can see, list, search or guess.
items.detail: Nothing flows down from it: shared starters and libraries are published by the product, public by nature.

items.title: Nothing crosses between Bases
items.value: No interface, search, graph, Flight line, cache, Depot path, webhook or metric crosses a Base, and “not found” looks the same as “not allowed”.
items.detail: Identifiers cannot be listed or guessed.

items.title: Proven by tests that gate every release
items.value: A suite tries every list, search, lookup, count, error, export and agent tool from one Base against another’s data.
items.detail: No outside customer is admitted until it passes.

items.title: A vendor console, separate from any Base
items.value: The service operator sees how many Bases exist, plans, usage trends, resource use and the health of the hosted side, and never repositories, Flight recorders, secrets, findings or traffic.
items.detail: It can suspend a Base, change a plan or publish a service notice.

items.title: A separate sign-in for the vendor
items.value: Vendor access is a different identity entered on purpose, with strong authentication, a stated reason and a session that ends by itself.
items.detail: An everyday account can never hold a vendor role.

items.title: Everything the vendor does shows in your Logbook
items.value: Every vendor action that touches your Base appears in your Base’s own Logbook, with who, why and when.
items.detail: You can see what was done to your Base without asking.

items.title: Support tickets from inside your Base
items.value: Open a ticket with a category and severity from your Base, or by email if the product is unreachable.
items.detail: The service operator lists tickets across Bases with their status and response clocks.

items.title: Support bundles you choose and preview
items.value: You pick from a checklist what goes in, secrets are removed, and you see a preview of exactly what will be sent before sending.
items.detail: Encrypted to the support team, kept for a stated time, and you can withdraw it.

items.title: A break-glass session you approve
items.value: If a bundle is not enough, you can grant a time-limited, read-only-by-default session for one problem, watch it live and end it at any moment.
items.detail: Every session is recorded where you can see it.

items.title: The same bundle for self-hosted installations
items.value: Self-hosted installations use the same command and send the file by their own channel, and an air-gapped customer can read it first.
items.detail: The same checklist, redaction and preview apply.

items.title: Proven in development, then production
items.value: Every release runs in a development installation first, and only builds that passed are promoted to the production one, which is also the hosted product.
items.detail: Production has encryption at rest, tested backups and at least two server replicas.

milestones.name: Zero-downtime delivery for anything, with Argo CD as a first-class citizen
milestones.promise: Every deployment, whatever it is made of, brings the new version up beside the old one, proves it, moves traffic or work over in steps you can see and control, keeps watching afterward and returns to the last good state by itself if things get worse.
milestones.audience: Enterprises that cannot afford to be hurt by a release yet want to deploy continuously, and any team that wants to see what is deployed and why something failed.
milestones.what: Milestone 8 gives delivery one model for everything: a plan, a mover that shifts traffic or work, proofs that say whether it is safe, controls you can press, and a record of the last stable state. The same model serves web services on Kubernetes, virtual machines behind a load balancer, serverless functions, queue workers and scheduled jobs. Argo CD becomes a first-class part of it: every application and its whole tree in one place, a plain sentence saying why something failed, and safe control. Everything is on by default and your team stays in charge; Launchway proposes changes and never rewrites your application.
scenarios: You describe a service in a few plain questions and get a plan with a picture. It is rehearsed in a safe Airfield, and written to Git for review.
A release reaches 5 percent of users, then 25, and each step shows the traffic you intended next to the traffic that actually arrived.
Thirty minutes after a release has reached everyone, error rates climb. Launchway sees it, returns to the last stable state, and the Logbook says who and what decided.
You switch on a Switch, errors rise, and Launchway switches it back off and tells you which toggle it was.
You open one page and see every Argo CD application, its parent and children, and a sentence saying why one of them cannot sync.
A rollout command that cannot work is never offered as a button.
