milestones.diagramNote: One journey for every kind of deployment. Only the shifter changes: a traffic split, a load balancer pool, a Holding pattern reader or a function alias.
done: The same plan runs a progressive rollout on Kubernetes, with every Argo Rollouts strategy covered and shown.
A seeded bad release is stopped and returned within the time the plan states, and a seeded good one is promoted, in the rehearsal Airfield and in the automated tests.
After the last step, the watch returns to the last stable state when signals worsen, and a Return to base after a success works from the interface, the API, the agent endpoint and the command line.
A toggle that causes errors is switched back automatically, and a configuration or secret change can be rolled and returned by a plan.
Every Argo CD application and its tree are visible, with a plain-language diagnosis for the common failures.
No control is offered that cannot work, and every control says what it will do and who may press it.
notIncluded: Making a change that is not backward compatible safe: Launchway warns and proposes, and cannot repair the design.
Guaranteeing full nines for a whole system from a rollout alone.
Replacing Argo CD or copying its screens: Launchway adds context and links to the original where it shows more.
Silently editing an application: every change is a proposal you accept, edit or decline.

groups.name: One model for every deployment
groups.blurb: First phase. A plan, a shifter, a proof, controls and a stable state, the same for every kind of workload.

items.title: Delivery plans
items.value: Describe how a release rolls out as a plan kept in Git: the steps, how much at each, what to check and how careful to be.
items.detail: You will be able to read a plan as a picture, review it like code, and reuse a standard plan from your organization.

items.title: Shifters
items.value: The part of a plan that moves traffic or work to the new version: a traffic split, a load balancer pool, a Holding pattern reader or a function alias.
items.detail: One interface lets every kind of workload take the same journey and show the same controls.

items.title: Proofs
items.value: Checks that say whether a step is safe: metrics, test transactions, network health and database health, each with a verdict in a sentence.
items.detail: A proof says not enough data rather than pass when a signal is too thin to judge.
items.needs: Delivery plans; guarded queries for monitoring data.

items.title: Guarded queries for monitoring data
items.value: Questions put to a metrics or log store pass through a guarded layer that limits what can be asked and how much comes back.
items.detail: Today the layer is being built. The rule is that monitoring data is a permission you grant and never a raw pass-through, and every proof and watch stands on it.

items.title: The stable state
items.value: For each Airfield Launchway records the version, settings, secret versions, toggles and routes that were known to work.
items.detail: The last good state is always one click, or one automatic decision, away.

items.title: Controls with consequences
items.value: Go, go all the way, pause, resume, stop and go back, try again, skip a step, set the amount by hand, restart and scale.
items.detail: Each button says in a sentence what it will do and who may press it, and each press is recorded in the Logbook.

items.title: Safeguards on by default
items.value: Every protection starts on and your team can tune or turn it off per project and Airfield; only a level above can require one.
items.detail: You stay in charge, and Launchway says plainly when a safeguard has been relaxed.

items.title: Rollout readiness scan
items.value: Launchway reads your application and tells you what stands in the way of a safe rollout, with changes it proposes.
items.detail: You accept, edit or decline each proposal; nothing is edited silently.

groups.name: Rollouts: every strategy, with an assistant
groups.blurb: First phase. Complete coverage of Argo Rollouts, created, seen and controlled from one panel.

items.title: Every rollout strategy
items.value: Pathfinder and blue-green, with all the step types, several analyses at once and experiments, created and shown in Launchway.
items.detail: Today Launchway reads a rollout; this makes it create and edit the files in Git, with every field accounted for.

items.title: An assistant for creating a rollout
items.value: A few plain questions (what is it, how do users reach it, how do we know it is healthy, how careful, who must clear it) produce a plan, a picture and files in Git.
items.detail: The proposal is rehearsed before it ever touches production.

items.title: The rollout panel
items.value: One panel shows the line of steps, where traffic really goes next to where it is meant to go, every check as it measures, old and new side by side, and events in time order.
items.detail: You will be able to see “10 percent intended, 9.4 percent measured” and what changed just before.

items.title: Rehearsal environments
items.value: Try a rollout in a short-lived Airfield with a traffic generator and injected faults before it reaches production.
items.detail: Rehearsal is a feature of the product, not only of its tests.
items.needs: An assistant for creating a rollout.

items.title: Return to any earlier version
items.value: Choose an earlier version and return to it, with what that will change spelled out first.
items.detail: A return by Git revert is the default; the engine’s own history is the emergency exit.

groups.name: Guarded after the deploy, and back to stable by itself
groups.blurb: First phase. The release is not finished when the last step is; the watch carries on and can return.

items.title: Roll back after a successful deployment
items.value: An emergency button that returns to the last stable state even after a rollout has succeeded.
items.detail: Available now: the control returns to the last stable state after a rollout has succeeded, with the same consequence text and Logbook entry as every other control.

items.title: The watch
items.value: After the last step, keep watching for a set time (30 minutes, for example) against a baseline of how the service normally behaves.
items.detail: The watch is the existing verification running after the final shift, with a plain “starting the return” decision if signals worsen.

items.title: Automatic return to stable
items.value: If error rates or other signals worsen during the watch, Launchway returns to the last stable state and says why.
items.detail: A cause outside the release, such as a failing dependency, is detected and does not trigger a pointless return.

items.title: Extend, end or override the watch
items.value: Lengthen a watch during a risky week, end it early, or override a return, each with a reason on the record.
items.detail: Production may require a person other than the one who started the release.

items.title: One timeline of what changed
items.value: Deployments, toggles, configuration and secrets on a single timeline, so what changed before it broke has an answer.
items.detail: It is the first place to look when a proof fails.

groups.name: Levers: toggles, configuration and secrets
groups.blurb: Second phase. Everything that can change behavior without a new build is versioned, rolled out and returnable.

items.title: A toggle service in the model
items.value: Toggles are known to Launchway, shown beside deployments on an Airfield's timeline, and offered for reverting with a Return to base.
items.detail: Rolling a toggle out in steps by a plan with proofs between them, and returning it with the rest of one stable-state record, are still to come.

items.title: Kill switches and automatic toggle-back
items.value: A toggle marked as a Master switch has a safe value, and turning it to that value is never held for an approval.
items.detail: Switching a toggle back automatically when errors rise after a change is still to come: today the change is shown as recent and a person reverts it.
items.needs: The watch; a toggle service in the model.

items.title: Stale-toggle hygiene
items.value: Toggles that have served one value to everyone for a month, have not been evaluated, or are past their removal date are noted on their page, never changed.
items.detail: A suggested pull request that removes the check and the toggle is still to come.
items.needs: A toggle service in the model.

items.title: Configuration and secrets as rollouts
items.value: A change to configuration or to a secret’s version is rolled out by a plan and can be returned.
items.detail: Secrets stay in their store; Launchway moves the reference and the version.

items.title: Drift detection for settings
items.value: Find configuration that differs between what is declared and what runs, and between Airfields.
items.detail: Drift is a finding with its cause, not an alarm without context.

items.title: Revert the latest change
items.value: When something breaks, one action reverts the most recent change on the timeline, whatever kind it was.
items.detail: The action says what it will undo before you press it.

groups.name: Hosts, serverless and other workloads
groups.blurb: Later phases. The same journey for virtual machines, bootable hosts, functions and workloads that are not web requests.

items.title: Hosts and pools
items.value: Pools of virtual machines or hosts deployed in batches behind a load balancer, with draining first.
items.detail: The first load balancer supported is a popular open-source one, then one cloud balancer.

items.title: Test transactions to a not-yet-live host
items.value: Send test requests to a new host before any user reaches it, and read the result as a proof.
items.detail: The host goes live only when its proofs pass.

items.title: Fleets of bootable-image hosts
items.value: Roll a new host image across a fleet in batches with a watch and a return.
items.detail: It joins the image work in Milestone 3.

items.title: Serverless and managed container services
items.value: Shift traffic between function versions and managed services using aliases and revisions, with proofs per version.
items.detail: Provider interfaces are tested against emulators in the automated tests.

items.title: Queue and stream consumers
items.value: Roll out a new version of a worker that reads a Holding pattern, by moving which copies read which part, and prove it with lag.
items.detail: A seeded backlog tests that the new version keeps up.

items.title: Long-lived connections and TCP
items.value: Drain connections that stay open for hours, and shift plain network services safely.
items.detail: It says honestly what cannot be made seamless.

items.title: Scheduled and batch jobs
items.value: Roll out a job that must run exactly once with a hand-over rather than an overlap.
items.detail: The plan changes shape and the answer is a short, controlled pause, not a claim of zero.

items.title: Safe changes to stateful services
items.value: Expand-then-contract steps for data, with a check that the old and new versions can both read what is written.
items.detail: It leans on the database work in Milestone 10.

groups.name: Argo CD, first class
groups.blurb: First phase for seeing and diagnosing, later for control and creating. Launchway does not replace Argo CD; it adds what no single Argo CD screen knows.

items.title: See every application and its tree
items.value: All applications from root to leaf, with a problem rolled up so a parent that looks fine while its children are not stands out first.
items.detail: You will be able to switch between a tree, a table and a by-environment view of the same nodes.

items.title: Every application in context
items.value: For each application: which change made it what it is, which run wrote that change, which version runs where and who owns it.
items.detail: It also lists the same service in other Airfields side by side.
items.needs: See every application and its tree.

items.title: A problem in one sentence
items.value: A diagnosis such as “Argo CD cannot build this application: a link points outside its folder”, with the evidence and the next step.
items.detail: When the cause is unknown it says so and what access would let it see more. A catalog of known causes is tested against real incidents.
items.needs: See every application and its tree.

items.title: Every item and its logs
items.value: Open any resource to see its events, manifest, desired against live, and logs including the previous container.
items.detail: Secrets appear by name only, and the access Launchway has is stated in a self-check.

items.title: Safe sync and control
items.value: Sync with a preview, refresh, stop a stuck sync, run a resource action, and pause automatic sync during an incident with a banner and a reminder.
items.detail: A button appears only if it will work, and each press is recorded.
items.needs: See every application and its tree.

items.title: Create and change through Git
items.value: An assistant writes an Application, an ApplicationSet or a Project into Git and opens a pull request, showing what will be created.
items.detail: Nothing is changed with a click against the cluster.
items.needs: Pull requests on the built-in host.

items.title: Adopt existing applications
items.value: Discover the applications you already have and map them to projects and Airfields without changing them.
items.detail: Discovery is opt-in and read-only.
items.needs: See every application and its tree.

items.title: Rollouts, sync and environments in one view
items.value: A joined timeline of a sync and its rollout, and a matrix of what version runs in each Airfield.
items.detail: Notification rules and Argo CD’s own notices appear in the same place.

milestones.name: Network and traffic you can see, from the edge to the workload
milestones.promise: For every application, Launchway answers one question: can it receive and serve requests right now, from where its users are, and if not, at which step does the route break?
milestones.audience: Operators and platform teams who today learn that the network is the problem by elimination, after an hour in four different tools.
milestones.what: Milestone 9 draws the route a request takes, from the edge provider through DNS, the gateway or load balancer, the firewall and the network policy to the service and its workloads, and shows the problems along it, worst first. It also learns what each application really depends on, handles several sites and failover, manages DNS records as part of a deployment, and understands service meshes, Istio most deeply. Everything is optional: Launchway sees only what you give it access to, says what it cannot see, and never captures the contents of traffic.
scenarios: Users in one region cannot reach an application. The path view shows the request reaching the gateway and stopping at a network policy, with the policy named.
You set up a connection to a metrics store and a cluster, and a setup assistant discovers what it can see and shows what each extra permission would add.
A deployment that needs a new name creates its DNS record, shows the difference first, and checks that every nameserver agrees afterward.
You ask to send only some clients to a new version, and Launchway shows which routing rule will match, in a plain explanation, before you apply it.
A site fails and traffic moves to the other one as rehearsed, with the lag and the order of events shown.

metrics, flows, mesh, probes"] -.-> Findings["Findings
worst first"] Findings -.-> GW

Sites and failover are shown and rehearsed.
notIncluded: Capturing the contents of traffic: Launchway sees addresses, names, ports, protocols, counts and timings only.
Replacing a mesh console, a firewall console or a protection service: Launchway shows their state and links to them.
Changing firewalls, DHCP or resolver settings, or DNS records Launchway does not own.
Issuing certificates itself in the first phases; it reads the certificate manager and shows the challenge state.

milestones.name: Databases that stay up, and database changes delivered like code
milestones.promise: Launchway keeps working when a database machine fails, loses no work it has acknowledged, and treats a change to your own databases as a first-class, checked, reversible part of a release.
milestones.audience: Teams that run Launchway for many people and teams whose releases include changes to their data.
milestones.what: Milestone 10 has two halves. The first makes Launchway’s own database highly available: one writer at a time, always with a copy guaranteed to be up to date, and software that promotes that copy automatically while Launchway waits, retries and buffers. The second treats a customer’s database as a known thing in an Airfield: a change set is checked before it runs, a backup is taken first, a standard tool applies it, and proofs watch the database during and after. Launchway is honest about limits: Return to base for data means roll forward, a compensating change or a restore.
scenarios: A database machine dies mid-push. Launchway serves again within a minute, no acknowledged push is lost, and no step is run twice.
You open a change set in a pull request and see the SQL it will run, what it will lock and whether it removes something a running version still uses.
A change runs through test, then production, only if its checksum is unchanged since you cleared it.
Two Airfields drift apart and Launchway shows exactly where.

flowchart TD Change["Change set
in Git"] --> Pre["Preflight

milestones.diagramNote: A database change as a plan like any other. Launchway never claims a data Return to base it cannot do.

An active-active multi-writer database as the default: it would trade correctness for speed.

milestones.name: Kubernetes, autoscaling, serverless and virtual machines, seen as one
milestones.promise: Launchway shows each workload in the context of the change that made it, answers why it is not healthy in one sentence across delivery, autoscaling, nodes, network and virtual machines, and delivers every kind of workload the same safe way.
milestones.audience: Application developers, on-call operators, platform engineers, security officers and managers, each of whom gets their own point of view on the same facts.
milestones.what: Milestone 11 starts from the change, not from the list of cluster objects. It adds clusters and a fleet view, a model of workloads that covers every common kind, a catalog of reasons something is unhealthy, autoscaling as a first-class view with advice that arrives as proposals, serverless including on-premises, and virtual machines on Kubernetes with full lifecycle and delivery. Raw depth in specialist tools stays in those tools, linked from the exact object. Launchway helps and does not take over: right-sizing, scaling and upgrade advice arrive as Git proposals.
scenarios: An on-call engineer opens a workload and reads one sentence: the new version cannot start because a node has no room, and the autoscaler cannot add one.
A developer sees only their service, with its rollouts, scaling and logs; a manager sees delivery flow and cost by team.
A scaling view shows why a workload is not scaling and proposes a change as a pull request.
A virtual machine’s disk import fails, and Launchway says the source address returned an error.
A virtual machine is released with the same plan, proofs and return as a container.

milestones.name: Security and trust: encrypted at rest, its own vault, and honest certification
milestones.promise: Everything Launchway holds is encrypted at rest with a key kept outside the database, an installation needs the fewest possible extra tools, and what is claimed about security is only what is true that day.
milestones.audience: Anyone who runs Launchway for a team that cares about security, and anyone evaluating it for a regulated Airfield.
milestones.what: Milestone 12 raises the foundation. A root key kept outside the database protects a small hierarchy of keys that protects every secret and stored file, so a database copy alone is useless. Launchway gets its own vault, and every built-in is optional: you can use a popular backend instead. Scans become gates with a stated policy, and the certification path is written down in an honest order.
scenarios: Someone gets a copy of the database. Without the installation key it is unreadable.
You rotate the installation key and nothing goes down.
A team with no other secret store keeps its secrets in Launchway’s vault, sealed by the same key hierarchy.
The doctor says plainly what is encrypted, what is not and how to fix it.
A signed release carries its provenance and an SBOM that anyone can verify.

Rotation and re-encryption happen without downtime, and an existing installation migrates without breaking.

items.value: Rotate keys, re-wrap them and re-encrypt over time while Launchway keeps serving.
items.detail: Backups and restores keep working across rotations.
items.needs: Encrypt stored files, logs and caches.

items.title: The doctor reports encryption plainly
items.value: A plain report of what is encrypted, what is not, and the one step to fix each gap.
items.detail: It never says encrypted when it is not.

items.title: Tamper-evident audit trail
items.value: the Logbook forms a chain so a deletion or an edit shows.
items.detail: The chain head can be exported for safekeeping.

items.title: Transport and sign-in hardening
items.value: Built-in transport encryption, refusal of unencrypted database connections, and sign-in rate limits with lockout.
items.detail: Safe defaults are on and your team can tune them.

items.title: Customer-held keys and deletion by key destruction
items.value: For the hosted service, keep logs and Cargo under a key you hold, and prove deletion by destroying it.
items.detail: Leaving is complete.

groups.name: Launchway’s own vault
groups.blurb: After encryption at rest. A minimum to install, and always optional.

items.title: A built-in secret store
items.value: Keep secrets in Launchway with policies and an audit trail, sealed by the same key hierarchy.
items.detail: It shares the database’s high availability.
items.needs: An installation key and a key hierarchy.

items.title: Popular backends instead
items.value: Use a popular secret backend instead, with the same behavior through one interface and a published parity matrix.
items.detail: Vault and OpenBao work today for Stations; this widens it.

items.title: Workload identity and dynamic credentials
items.value: Short-lived credentials issued to a run for the time it needs them.
items.detail: A step never holds a long-lived secret.

items.title: Built in by default, a backend by choice
items.value: Every dependency has a built-in default and a popular external option, with the trade-offs written down.
items.detail: The only things required remain a database and Git.

groups.name: The security program
groups.blurb: Ongoing. Scans are gates, releases are verifiable and the program is written down.

items.title: Security scans as a program
items.value: Code, dependency, secret, image, chart and manifest scanning, fuzzing and security headers run on every change.
items.detail: Gates have a stated policy and an expiring exception process.

items.title: A security policy and threat model
items.value: A published policy for reporting a problem and a written threat model that shows what Launchway defends against.
items.detail: Both are kept current with the code.

items.title: A hardening guide and installation benchmark
items.value: A guide and an automated check for how to harden an installation, in the style of a standard benchmark.
items.detail: The doctor runs the check.

items.title: Penetration testing and incident response
items.value: Independent testing, a response runbook and a public summary of what was found.
items.detail: Scheduled after encryption at rest and the vault ship.

groups.name: Certification, in an honest order
groups.blurb: Practices first, then certificates earned. Launchway never claims one it has not earned.

items.title: Open source security badges and a scorecard
items.value: The open-source security best-practices badge and a public scorecard with a target.
items.detail: Some checks need people and time and will lag honestly.

items.title: Build provenance, level two now and three next
items.value: Signed provenance for every release, then a build platform that isolates runs and keeps signing keys from build steps.
items.detail: Anyone can verify it.

items.title: An independent security audit
items.value: A specialist firm audits the server, sign-in, Station protocol, encryption and chart defaults, and a summary is published.
items.detail: It follows encryption at rest and the vault.
items.needs: An installation key and a key hierarchy.

items.title: A validated cryptographic build
items.value: A build variant that uses a validated cryptographic module, claimed only for that variant.
items.detail: The default build never claims it.

items.title: Hosted service attestation
items.value: An independent report on the hosted service’s controls, then a longer-period report.
items.detail: It follows once the hosted service has run.
items.needs: Hosted service that holds nothing sensitive.

items.title: Responsibility matrix for regulated customers
items.value: A table of which payment-card and health-data requirements Launchway’s features help you meet and which remain yours.
items.detail: Launchway supports compliance work; it is not a certification.

groups.name: The same standards for every repository
groups.blurb: The scans Launchway holds itself to are offered to every repository it hosts or builds, built in, with nothing to install and every check a switch.

items.title: A profile for each repository
items.value: Launchway looks at what a repository holds, such as Go, a Dockerfile or Helm charts, and attaches the checks that fit, each with the reason it was recommended.
items.detail: Checks are on from the first push.

items.title: Every check on, advice or block
items.value: Each check is off, advice or a block, at any level and per repository, and a level above can require a minimum.
items.detail: The team in charge of a repository keeps the choice unless a level above locks it.

items.title: Vulnerability, secret, dependency and license checks
items.value: Vulnerability and secret scans, dependency and license checks, and best practices for each language run for every repository, not only Launchway’s own.
items.detail: Checks are visible steps, never hidden magic.

items.title: Language profiles
items.value: Go, Python, JavaScript and TypeScript, Java, Dockerfile and Helm come first; Kotlin, C#, Rust, Ruby, PHP, C and C++, shell, Terraform and Ansible follow.
items.detail: Each profile brings starter files the team may change.

items.title: Findings in one list
items.value: Every check reports into one findings list with what it is, where, how serious, how sure the tool is, how to fix it and when it was first seen.
items.detail: Findings show on the pull request and in the repository, team and Wing views.

items.title: Fix proposals as pull requests
items.value: Launchway opens a pull request for a dependency bump, a base image update, a formatter run, a pinned digest or a hardened setting, and never edits silently.
items.detail: Limits keep teams from being flooded, and automatic merging is off by default.

items.title: Safe defaults and a break-glass path
items.value: A new critical or high vulnerability with a fix, or a secret, blocks a merge to a protected branch; everything else is advice; every block has a reasoned, expiring way through.
items.detail: Only new findings block, so an old backlog does not stop work.

items.title: Exceptions with an owner and an expiry
items.value: Waive a finding with a reason, an owner and an end date, and optionally say why it cannot be exploited, in a format you can publish.
items.detail: When an exception expires the finding counts again.

items.title: Stored parts lists rechecked against new advisories
items.value: When a new advisory is published, Launchway says which repositories and running versions are affected without anyone pushing a commit.
items.detail: Stored software bills of materials are matched again each time an advisory appears.

items.title: Patch everything affected by an advisory
items.value: Start a campaign that opens one fix per affected repository and tracks it until the new version is seen running.
items.detail: A page shows each repository’s state, owner and deadline.

items.title: Standards kept in Git, edited in either place
items.value: A level’s standards can live as files in a repository that level owns, so a change to them is reviewed like any other change, and the same settings stay editable in the interface, with the two kept in step.
items.detail: Teams control their own repositories: every default can be changed, the nearest level wins, and a level above can set a floor. Built and tested, not yet merged: the file `.launchway/standards.yaml` is read from the default branch, validated in plain words, and settings by level, with locks, are edited in Settings.
items.needs: Every check on, advice or block.

items.title: Adapters for the tools teams already pay for
items.value: The results of commercial Cargo repositories, code-analysis and security products come into the same findings list, gates and reports as the free, open defaults.
items.detail: The free defaults always work with nothing else; an adapter only adds to them.

items.title: A standards home and a posture view
items.value: See a score with what moves it, the top risks, repositories without a profile and trends, per Wing, team and repository.
items.detail: The score is a view, never a gate by itself. The first slice is built and not yet merged: which repositories have which checks, and each project's open findings over time with the mean time to fix. A score is not built.

items.title: Evidence for auditors
items.value: A report for a period shows which checks were on, evidence that they ran, findings and fixes, and exceptions.
items.detail: Evidence support only; not a certification.

items.title: Checks that run on your side
items.value: On the hosted service checks run on your Stations, so source code and finding detail stay with you.
items.detail: Only counts and summaries cross to the hosted side.

principles.title: Everything, without the mess
principles.value: Every feature uses the same objects, permissions, audit trail and policy point, and nothing switched off appears in the menus.

principles.title: One way in, every way in
principles.value: A wizard for each task, with the same operation in the HTTP API, the agent endpoint, the command line and Terraform.

principles.title: Only a database and Git
principles.value: Everything else is built in; outside integrations stay optional.

principles.title: Boring upgrades
principles.value: One binary and a database, additive migrations, an older binary running on a newer schema, and Return to base by image.

principles.title: High availability and security are part of done
principles.value: A feature says what happens when a server, the database or a Station dies, and who may do what, before it merges.

principles.title: Honest status
principles.value: An item is available only when it is merged, tested and documented. Order is by value and is not a schedule.

principles.title: Security first
principles.value: Everything Launchway holds is encrypted at rest, every part runs with least privilege, and the secure choice is the default.

principles.title: Help, never enforce or overwrite
principles.value: Launchway explains, proposes and previews. It never rewrites your application or infrastructure silently; you accept, edit or decline.

principles.title: Safeguards on, the team in charge
principles.value: Every protection starts on and your team may tune or turn it off. Only a level above you, such as the Wing for production, can require one.

principles.title: Never a button that does not work
principles.value: An action that cannot work here is absent or shown unavailable with the reason. A risky action that is allowed asks first, in plain words.

principles.title: Everything optional, with built-in defaults
principles.value: Each capability has a built-in default and a popular backend you can use instead, so an installation needs the fewest tools.

principles.title: The hosted service holds nothing sensitive
principles.value: Your network and your secrets stay with you, seen only through a small program that runs on your side.

principles.title: Accessible to everyone
principles.value: Automated checks hold every screen, and the API, agent endpoint and command line, to a top-tier standard for keyboard, screen reader and contrast.

principles.title: Simple to install, nothing assumed
principles.value: A handful of values, no secrets manager or identity provider required, and a guided first sign-in that is the same for everyone.

principles.title: Every customer’s Base is walled off, and proven
principles.value: Isolation between customers is not a promise: tests try every route from one Base into another and gate every release.

principles.title: A cache only makes a build faster
principles.value: It may never change a build’s result: what can change is looked up again, and a Sortie says when it cannot be sure.

principles.title: The system works out the order; a person can always override
principles.value: Build order, release order and branching patterns are worked out from your code, shown with their reasons, and open to correction.

items: Releases: make, publish and promote a release with its notes, Cargo and image digests; a matrix of what runs where; checklists, change windows, freezes and a calendar; Formations; and a report of frequency, lead time, change failure rate and time to restore.
The hosted service now starts with small teams: sign up and go, with a passkey or authenticator app and recovery codes, and no text-message codes.

Three ways to run one product are described, with easy, previewed moves between them: fully hosted, hosted with your own machines (including files that stay on your machines behind an encrypted relay, with copies on two machines), and self-hosted.
Hosted size ceilings with notices and nothing held hostage, a hosted service that is never public file storage, the wall between Bases proven by tests, and outsiders let in stage by stage.
A free plan principle: every feature on, spend limit at zero. Prices and numeric limits are not decided and are not listed.

Builds across a team’s machines by free processor and memory, load-aware Stations on personal machines, fair use, matrix builds, shared step templates, a starter library, detection, a gallery, launchway init and an editor schema (being built now).

Statuses corrected against the code: only what is on the main branch is Available. Encryption at rest, built-in accounts, the guided installer, queueing and limits, path filters, restricted pull requests, deploy health checks, GitOps write-back, notifications, offline validation and Maintenance are built and in final integration.
New: a short, honest “Where Launchway stands today” section, and the order we are building in.

Steps that cannot start for lack of room now wait with a reason, runs have limits and a fair order, triggers and steps have path filters, and pull requests from automation accounts run restricted until a maintainer approves.
Delivery gaps closed: a built-in health proof for verify steps, GitOps write-back races, tags with digests and hosted repositories, notifications, template defaults and offline validate.

Install and upgrade: `launchway install` for a laptop, a server or Kubernetes, a first-run guide in the web interface, secrets the chart makes once and keeps, encryption of stored secrets under a root key, and built-in Maintenance are in this build; waiting for room, limits, path filters and restricted pull requests as well.

strong: Delivery with verification and Return to base: a deployment is checked, and you can return to the last good state even after it succeeded.
Failures that explain themselves: a failed Sortie says why, with the evidence, and re-runs from the failed step.
Pipelines you can see: steps drawn the way they run, and a change followed from idea to running software.
Runs on your own hardware: one program and a database, with no outside service required.
missing: A large library of ready-made steps and starters: a first set is being built now.
Hosted Stations: they come last in the opening of the hosted service.
Matrix builds: being built now, not yet merged.
Maturity: Launchway is young, has few users and has not been through an independent security audit or a certification.
